children.title: Compact Convex-Domain Regime
children.top_down_role: The bounded-domain setting underlying the classical linear-minimization framework.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bounded convexity alone does not ensure oracle attainment: on \(C=(0,1)\), the continuous linear functional \(s\mapsto s\) has infimum \(0\), but no point of \(C\) attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded but nonclosed convex domain can have a finite linear infimum that is not attained.

Compact Convex-Domain Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bounded-domain regime for classical conditional-gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. Its diameter \(D:=\sup\{\lVert x-y\rVert:x,y\in C\}\) is finite, and every continuous linear functional attains its minimum on \(C\). Thus, for each \(g\in E^*\), the linear-minimization set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\) is nonempty. The compact convex-domain regime is the constrained problem \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) under these geometric conditions; existence of a minimizer additionally follows whenever \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible set is nonempty, compact, and convex, so it has finite diameter and every linear-minimization oracle call attains a solution.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(C\subset E\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D<\infty\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\neq\varnothing\) for every \(g\in E^*\).

notation.meaning: dual space of continuous linear functionals on E
diameter of the feasible set C

review_flags: Relevant conditional-gradient source locator is absent from the supplied inventory.
standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional compactness guarantees attainment of continuous linear objectives.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness and oracle-attainment claims are standard and fit the condition container, but the record cites no source or inspectable locator. The LaTeX statement additionally asserts existence of a minimizer for lower-semicontinuous f, while the plain statement omits that claim. Source support and aligned formulations are required before acceptance.

children.title: Strong-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective-growth settings relevant to accelerated conditional-gradient behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-growth conditions relating objective residual to distance from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty and let \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) be attained on the nonempty set \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). For constants \(\mu>0\) and \(p\ge 1\), the problem satisfies \((\mu,p)\)-growth when, for every \(x\in C\), \[f(x)-f^*\ge \frac{\mu}{p}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p.\] The case \(p=2\) is quadratic growth. This condition concerns growth away from \(X^*\) and does not, by itself, assert strong convexity of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective error dominates a positive power of the distance to the solution set; quadratic growth is the exponent-two case.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is nonempty.

notation.meaning: distance from x to the solution set in the ambient norm

review_flags: The title admits competing meanings, including quadratic growth, strong convexity, and geometric strong convexity.
Chosen version is the power-growth condition suggested by the Growth-Sharpness parent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A power-growth condition is a plausible condition for this leaf, but "strong growth" has competing meanings in optimization, including quadratic growth, strong convexity, and geometric strong convexity. No citation identifies the taxonomy's intended convention, exponent range, or normalization, so the selected formulation cannot be validated.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\max\{x^2,|x|\}\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*=f(x)\ge x^2=\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})^2\), while \(f\) is not strongly convex.
review_flags: The separation of quadratic growth from strong convexity is mathematically correct.
Publication is deferred because the leaf's intended strong-growth convention is unresolved.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional separation of quadratic growth from strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex function \(f(x)=\max\{x^2,|x|\}\) has unique minimizer \(0\), satisfies \(f(x)-f^*\ge\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})^2\), and is not strongly convex because it is affine on \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex objective can have global quadratic growth while containing an affine segment and therefore failing strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Without Strong Convexity

intermediate_metadata.reason: The phrase Strong-Growth Regimes is materially ambiguous among power growth, quadratic growth, strong convexity, and conditional-gradient geometric strong convexity. Moreover, the proposed power-growth convention becomes identical to the Sharpness Regimes seed after reciprocal-exponent conversion, defeating the sibling partition. Sharpness and rate implications are excluded to siblings; general strong-convexity theory is excluded to its dedicated topic.

children.title: Sharpness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sharp objective landscapes supporting stronger local or global guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölderian sharpness expressed as an error bound from objective residual to solution distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*\) be attained over a nonempty feasible set \(C\), with solution set \(X^*\neq\varnothing\). For constants \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in(0,1]\), the problem has \((c,\theta)\)-sharpness on a set \(U\subseteq C\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le c\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)^\theta\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] If \(U=C\), the condition is global; if \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\), it is local. The value \(\theta=1\) gives linear sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharpness bounds distance to the solution set by a power of objective error, either locally or globally.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
\(c>0\), \(\theta\in(0,1]\), and \(U\subseteq C\).

notation.meaning: region on which sharpness is asserted

Chosen convention is the Hölder error-bound form.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hölder error-bound formulation is mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf, but sharpness conventions use differing exponent directions and normalizations. No cited source or locator establishes that this is the intended convention or that theta is restricted to (0,1].

children.title: Rate Implications Across Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergence consequences associated with differing growth-strength regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Rate Implications Across Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic rate conversion from a descent recurrence, separated from algorithm-specific constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_t:=f(x_t)-f^*\ge 0\). Suppose that, after any required burn-in, an algorithm satisfies \(h_{t+1}\le h_t-a h_t^q\) with \(a>0\) and \(q\ge 1\), and assume \(a h_t^{q-1}\le 1\). If \(q=1\), then \(h_t\le (1-a)^{t-t_0}h_{t_0}\). If \(q>1\), then \[h_t\le\left(h_{t_0}^{1-q}+a(q-1)(t-t_0)\right)^{-1/(q-1)}.\] Consequently, growth or sharpness assumptions improve rates only after they yield such a stronger residual recurrence for the particular conditional-gradient variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear residual recurrence gives geometric convergence; a higher-power recurrence gives an explicit polynomial rate. Growth conditions matter through the recurrence they enable.
assumptions_latex: \(h_t\ge 0\) and \(h_{t+1}\le h_t-a h_t^q\) for all \(t\ge t_0\).

notation.meaning: first iteration for which the recurrence holds

children.title: Interior-Solution Regime
children.top_down_role: Solution locations separated from the feasible-region boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Solution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution location relative to the relative interior of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty and convex, and suppose \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\). The problem is in the interior-solution regime when \(X^*\cap\operatorname{ri}(C)\neq\varnothing\). A quantitative interior-margin version requires an optimizer \(x^*\in X^*\cap\operatorname{ri}(C)\) and a radius \(r>0\) such that \(\{x^*+u:u\in\operatorname{aff}(C)-x^*,\ \lVert u\rVert\le r\}\subseteq C\). The margin distinguishes strict interiority from solutions merely approaching the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At least one optimizer lies in the relative interior; quantitatively, a positive relative ball around that optimizer remains feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset E\) is nonempty and convex.
\(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).

children.title: Boundary-Solution Regime
children.top_down_role: Solution locations lying on proper faces or exposed boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Solution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution location on the relative boundary of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty and convex, and suppose \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\). The problem is in the boundary-solution regime when every optimizer lies on the relative boundary, namely \(X^*\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(C):=\operatorname{cl}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(C)\). For a closed convex set and a chosen \(x^*\in X^*\), the active geometry may be represented by the minimal face \(F^*\) of \(C\) containing \(x^*\); a proper active face satisfies \(F^*\neq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every optimizer lies on the relative boundary, and a chosen optimizer belongs to a proper minimal face of the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X^*\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(C)\); the minimal face containing a boundary optimizer is proper.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stability of linear-minimization outputs on a polyhedral exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a compact polytope and \(F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g^*,s\rangle\) a proper exposed face. If the vertices outside \(F^*\) have positive objective separation \(\delta\), then every minimizer for all sufficiently small dual-norm perturbations of \(g^*\) remains in \(F^*\). For a general compact convex set lacking a positive separation margin, such stability need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive exposing margin makes a polytope's linear-oracle selection of an active face stable under small changes of the linear objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Exposed-Face Oracle Stability
Transitions Near Active Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stabilization of the minimal face under positive separation from competing faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a polytope, let \(F^*\) be a proper face, and let \(x^*\in\operatorname{ri}(F^*)\). Define the relative-face margin \(r_F:=\operatorname{dist}(x^*,\operatorname{rbd}(F^*))\), measured in \(\operatorname{aff}(F^*)\). If \(r_F>0\), then every \(x\in F^*\) with \(\lVert x-x^*\rVert<r_F\) remains in \(\operatorname{ri}(F^*)\). Nevertheless, arbitrarily small ambient perturbations from \(x^*\) may leave \(F^*\) whenever \(F^*\neq C\). Thus local active-face stability requires both proximity and membership in the identified face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a proper active face, a positive relative margin stabilizes face membership; small ambient perturbations can still leave that face.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-dimensional polytope and \(F^*\) is a proper face.
\(x^*\in\operatorname{ri}(F^*)\) and \(r_F>0\).

children.title: Exact Linear-Minimization Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact feasible-set access through linear optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable on a convex set containing compact convex \(C\).
\(x\in C\), \(s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in C}\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle\), and \(f^*=\min_C f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-suboptimality and first-order-optimality certificate generated by an exact LMO call.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact Frank-Wolfe gap satisfies \(0\le f(x)-f^*\le G(x)\). Moreover, \(G(x)=0\) if and only if \(\langle\nabla f(x),v-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(v\in C\); for convex differentiable \(f\), this condition is equivalent to global optimality over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact Frank-Wolfe gap upper-bounds convex primal error and vanishes exactly at first-order optimal points.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines relative strength by uniform oracle simulation, independently of a particular conditional-gradient algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two oracle interfaces \(\mathcal O_1\) and \(\mathcal O_2\) on the same query class \(\mathcal Q\), write \(\mathcal O_1\succeq\mathcal O_2\) when there exists a uniform procedure that, for every \(q\in\mathcal Q\), produces a response admissible for \(\mathcal O_2(q)\) using finitely many calls to \(\mathcal O_1\) and permitted auxiliary computation. The comparison is quantitative if functions \(N\) and \(T\) bound, respectively, the number of calls and auxiliary cost. Mutual simulation, \(\mathcal O_1\succeq\mathcal O_2\) and \(\mathcal O_2\succeq\mathcal O_1\), defines interface equivalence under the declared computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One oracle interface is at least as strong as another if it can uniformly simulate every valid response using finitely many calls and allowed auxiliary computation.
assumptions_latex: Both interfaces accept queries from a common declared class \(\mathcal Q\).
The admissible auxiliary operations and accuracy convention are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relation \(\succeq\) is reflexive and transitive, and mutual simulation defines an equivalence relation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\), a vector \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\) minimizes \(\langle g,s\rangle\) over \(C\) if and only if each \(s_i\) minimizes \(\langle g_i,z_i\rangle\) over \(C_i\). Block-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes deterministic, randomized, and greedy choices of the block queried at each iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) blocks, a block-selection regime is a sequence of rules producing \(i_t\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) from the iteration history \(\mathcal F_t\). It is cyclic when \(i_t=1+(t\bmod m)\) after a fixed relabeling; randomized with full support when \(i_t\) is sampled conditionally with probabilities \(p_{t,i}=\mathbb P(i_t=i\mid\mathcal F_t)\) satisfying \(p_{t,i}\ge p_{\min}>0\); and greedy when \(i_t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_i G_i(x_t)\), where \(G_i(x_t)\) is the block linearization gap. Each regime determines which block-restricted oracle may be called at iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selection regime chooses the queried block cyclically, randomly with positive coverage, or greedily by the largest block gap.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact order-k atomic oracle for a finite atom set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_N\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be finite and let \(1\le k\le N\). children.title: Nearest-Extreme-Point Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces selecting extreme points through proximity-based criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\operatorname{ext}(C)\) is nonempty and compact.
Distance is Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between Euclidean nearest-extreme-point queries and regularized linear scoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Euclidean distance, nearest-extreme-point selection is equivalent to minimizing \(\tfrac12\|v\|_2^2-\langle y,v\rangle\) over \(v\in V\). If every \(v\in V\) has the same Euclidean norm, this reduces to the exact linear query \(\min_{v\in V}\langle-y,v\rangle\), equivalently an LMO over compact convex \(C\). Without equal norms the quadratic term is essential: for \(C=[-1,2]\) and \(y=0\), the nearest extreme point is \(-1\), whereas the linear query with covector \(-y=0\) admits both extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean nearest-extreme-point selection is a norm-regularized linear problem and becomes an ordinary LMO only under equal extreme-point norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Linear Representation of Nearest Extreme Points
Nearest-Extreme-Point Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric projection of a query point onto the extreme points of a compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, let \(V=\operatorname{ext}(C)\), and fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). A nearest-extreme-point oracle receives \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) and returns \(v_y\in V\) satisfying \[\|v_y-y\|=\min_{v\in V}\|v-y\|.\] For a polytope, \(V\) is finite and the minimum is attained. The oracle differs from a linear-minimization oracle: it optimizes metric distance to the query rather than a linear score, and neither response generally determines the other without additional geometric computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns an extreme point closest to a query in a fixed norm; this is generally different from linear minimization.
assumptions_latex: The extreme-point set \(V=\operatorname{ext}(C)\) is nonempty and compact.
The norm \(\|\cdot\|\) is fixed as part of the interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The response \(v_y\) minimizes distance from \(y\) over all extreme points of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Extreme-point set of the feasible domain.
Nearest extreme point returned for query y.

review_flags: exact_interface_ambiguous: nearest-extreme-point oracles may instead include a linear or quadratic regularization parameter

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended nearest-extreme-point interface requires a specialized source because related interfaces may instead use regularized linear or quadratic queries. Moreover, compactness of C alone does not establish compactness of ext(C); attainment requires the separately listed compactness assumption on V, which should be incorporated directly into the definition.

children.title: Rich-Oracle Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Information gains, computational costs, plus representational effects of stronger oracle access.

assumptions_latex: A rich oracle returns \(k\) separately addressable atoms in an explicit-output representation.
Writing or reading one atom identifier has positive unit cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive cost boundary for explicitly returned rich atomic responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an explicit-output model, an oracle returning \(k\) separately addressable atoms incurs \(\Omega(k)\) response-writing cost, and an algorithm inspecting all returned atoms incurs \(\Omega(k)\) response-reading cost, even if the interaction counts as one oracle call. Thus oracle-call complexity can conceal a factor proportional to response size. The bound does not apply unchanged to a succinct or lazy representation that need not be fully expanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A call returning k explicit atoms has at least linear output or full-inspection cost, so call counts can hide the cost of richer responses.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Rich-Response Size Bound
Rich-Oracle Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates oracle informativeness from per-call and end-to-end computational cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a rich oracle \(\mathcal R\) returns a response from which a valid linear-minimization atom can be extracted for every linear query \(g\). Then \(\mathcal R\succeq\mathcal L\), where \(\mathcal L\) denotes the ordinary linear-minimization interface, and any algorithm using \(q\) calls to \(\mathcal L\) can be implemented with at most \(q\) calls to \(\mathcal R\), plus extraction work. This interface dominance alone implies no dominance in total runtime: if one call costs \(c_{\mathcal R}\), iteration counts are \(q_{\mathcal R}(\varepsilon)\), and auxiliary cost is \(h_{\mathcal R}(\varepsilon)\), the relevant total is \(q_{\mathcal R}(\varepsilon)c_{\mathcal R}+h_{\mathcal R}(\varepsilon)\), which may exceed the corresponding linear-oracle total.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A richer oracle can simulate an ordinary LMO, but fewer iterations need not mean lower runtime because rich calls and response processing may cost more.
assumptions_latex: Every response of \(\mathcal R\) permits extraction of an exact linear-minimization atom.
Both implementations use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interface dominance \(\mathcal R\succeq\mathcal L\) does not by itself order end-to-end computational costs.

notation.meaning: Total rich-oracle cost model at accuracy epsilon.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle reductions and end-to-end cost accounting distinguish information strength from implementation cost

children.title: Finite Atomic Domains
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions represented through explicitly finite atom collections.

assumptions_latex: The generating set \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The domain \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) is a compact polytope and has the same minimum linear score as \(\mathcal A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary finite-dimensional convex-hull and linear-functional facts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex feasible domains generated by finitely many explicitly or implicitly represented atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_N\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and finite. Its finite atomic domain is \[C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j a_j:\lambda_j\ge 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=1\right\}.\] The set \(C\) is a compact polytope. For every \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), linear minimization over \(C\) reduces to atom selection: \[\min_{x\in C}\langle g,x\rangle=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle g,a\rangle.\] The generating set need not be minimal; atoms that are not extreme points may be removed without changing \(C\) when they lie in the convex hull of the remaining atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite atomic domain is the convex hull of finitely many atoms; linear minimization over it reduces to selecting a lowest-scoring atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Atomic Domains

children.title: Polyhedral Domains
children.top_down_role: Polytope-based feasible regions with potentially implicit extreme-point structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Polyhedra Can Defeat the LMO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundedness failure for the compact polyhedral conditional-gradient interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Boundedness cannot be removed from the compact polyhedral-domain interface. For \(P=\mathbb R\) and \(g=1\),
\[
\inf_{x\in P}gx=-\infty,
\]
so \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}gx=\varnothing\). More generally, if a polyhedron has a recession direction \(d\) with \(\langle g,d\rangle<0\), then its linear objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded polyhedron need not admit an LMO answer; a negative-cost recession direction makes the linear objective unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is permitted to be an unbounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P}\langle g,x\rangle\) may equal \(-\infty\), so a globally defined compact-domain LMO need not exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polyhedra Can Defeat the LMO

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Minimizers Form an Exposed Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of LMO outputs on a compact polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope and \(g\in\mathbb R^n\). Then
\[
F_g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}\langle g,x\rangle
\]
is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\). It is a polytope and contains a vertex of \(P\); hence an LMO may return a vertex, although the minimizing vertex need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear minimization over a compact polytope exposes a nonempty face containing a vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(g\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_g\) is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\) and \(F_g\cap\operatorname{ext}(P)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: face exposed by minimizing the covector g

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Minimizers Form an Exposed Face
Polyhedral Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral feasible sets in equivalent inequality and finite-vertex forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Bx\le d\}\) be nonempty and bounded. Then \(P\) has finitely many extreme points \(V=\operatorname{ext}(P)\) and admits the vertex representation \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V).\] Conversely, the convex hull of every nonempty finite subset of \(\mathbb R^n\) is a bounded polyhedron and therefore admits a representation by finitely many linear inequalities. Hence compact polyhedral domains and finite atomic domains describe the same class of feasible sets, although their input encodings and the costs of linear minimization may differ substantially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty bounded inequality-defined polyhedron is the convex hull of finitely many vertices, and every finite convex hull has a finite inequality representation.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is finite-dimensional.
The polyhedron \(P=\{x:Bx\le d\}\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a finite set \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\), and the converse representation also holds.

notation.meaning: Finite system of componentwise linear inequalities.

children.top_down_role: Navigation across explicit generator lists plus implicit polyhedral descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Atom versus Implicit-Polytope Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares V-representation by atoms with H-representation by inequalities for one compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compact polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) may be supplied explicitly by atoms, \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_N\}\), or implicitly by inequalities, \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Bx\le d\}\). These representations define the same geometric class but different computational interfaces. In the explicit representation, \[\min_{x\in P}\langle g,x\rangle=\min_{1\le j\le N}\langle g,a_j\rangle.\] In the implicit representation, the same query is a linear program with constraints \(Bx\le d\). Conversion between complete vertex and inequality descriptions can require output exponentially larger than the input, so representation equivalence does not imply comparable encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex lists and inequality systems represent the same compact polytopes, but they induce different LMO implementations and may differ exponentially in description size.
assumptions_latex: The polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and compact.
Each displayed representation is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two encodings describe the same class of sets, while linear-oracle implementation and representation size remain encoding-dependent.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: V- and H-representations are standard polyhedral encodings; conversion may have exponential output size

children.title: Infinite Atomic Domains
children.top_down_role: Convex-hull models with continuously indexed or infinite atom families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional failure of closure-free representation and atomic LMO attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{1/k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)=(0,1]\), whereas
\[
C=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\mathcal A)=[0,1].
\]
For \(g=1\),
\[
\min_{x\in C}x=0=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}a,
\]
but no atom attains the infimum. Thus closure and the distinction between atomic infimum and attained atomic minimum can both be essential for a noncompact infinite atom family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The atoms 1/k generate (0,1] before closure and [0,1] after closure; minimizing the identity reaches zero on the closed domain but on no atom.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{1/k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R\).
\(C=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=[0,1]\), \(\min_{x\in C}x=0\), and \(\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}a=0\) is not attained.

notation.meaning: noncompact infinite atom family missing its limit atom
closed convex hull of the atom family

knowledge_statements.title: Closure and Atomic-Attainment Failure
Infinite Atomic Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex-hull models generated by infinitely or continuously indexed atom families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be an infinite atom family. Its infinite atomic domain is \(C=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\mathcal A)\). If \(\mathcal A\) is compact, then \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) is compact, every \(x\in C\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) atoms, and for every \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\min_{x\in C}\langle g,x\rangle=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle g,a\rangle.\] Without compactness, the closure may be essential and the infimum of the atomic linear problem need not be attained by an atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite atomic domain is a closed convex hull; compact atom families ensure finite atomic decompositions and attainment of linear minima.
assumptions_latex: The atom family \(\mathcal A\) lies in the finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^n\).
Compactness of \(\mathcal A\) is assumed for the attainment and finite-representation conclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For compact \(\mathcal A\), the domain is compact, each point uses at most \(n+1\) atoms, and linear minimization reduces to an attained atomic minimum.

notation.meaning: Closed convex hull of the atom family.
Infinite or continuously indexed atom family.

children.title: Product Domains
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions formed from Cartesian products of component domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact diameter decomposition in block Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^mC_i\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_i}\), with \(\|x\|_2^2=\sum_i\|x_i\|_2^2\). For nonempty compact factors,
\[
\operatorname{diam}_2(C)^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{diam}_2(C_i)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the block Euclidean norm, the squared diameter of a compact product is the sum of the squared factor diameters.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is nonempty and compact.
The product carries the standard block Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Diameter of a Product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point structure of a finite Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty compact convex sets \(C_i\) in finite-dimensional real vector spaces,
\[
\operatorname{ext}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^mC_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ext}(C_i).
\]
Thus a point of the product is extreme exactly when every component is extreme, and an extreme LMO answer can be assembled from extreme component answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of a finite Cartesian product are exactly the tuples of extreme points of its factors.
assumptions_latex: Every \(C_i\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.

notation.meaning: set of extreme points of a convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Points of Product Domains
Product Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian products whose linear-minimization oracle decomposes exactly across component domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty compact convex sets for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Their product domain is \[C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in C_i\}.\] For a block covector \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\), linear minimization decomposes as \[\min_{x\in C}\langle g,x\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m\min_{x_i\in C_i}\langle g_i,x_i\rangle.\] Consequently, choosing independently \(s_i\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in C_i}\langle g_i,x_i\rangle\) yields \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle g,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product domain is a Cartesian product of component sets, and its linear-minimization problem separates exactly into independent component problems.
assumptions_latex: Each component set \(C_i\) is nonempty and compact.
The objective pairs blockwise as \(\langle g,x\rangle=\sum_i\langle g_i,x_i\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Componentwise linear minimizers combine into a global linear minimizer over \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\).

children.title: Decomposable Domains

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and Convexity of Decomposable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural inheritance for a finite sum of linear images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\geq1\), let \(U_i:E_i\to E\) be linear maps between finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and let every \(C_i\subset E_i\) be nonempty and compact. Then
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^mU_iC_i=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\right\}
\]
is nonempty and compact. If every \(C_i\) is convex, then \(C\) is convex. Compactness yields attainment of linear minima, while component convexity places \(C\) in the usual convex conditional-gradient setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of linear images of nonempty compact sets is compact; convex component sets also yield a convex decomposable domain.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq1\) is finite.
Each \(U_i:E_i\to E\) is linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
Each \(C_i\) is nonempty and compact; convexity is additionally assumed for the convexity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\sum_{i=1}^mU_iC_i\) is nonempty and compact, and is convex if every \(C_i\) is convex.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the linear images of the component sets

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness and Convexity of Decomposable Domains
Decomposable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-image decomposition, broader than a Cartesian-product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E,E_1,\ldots,E_m\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let each \(C_i\subset E_i\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(U_i:E_i\to E\) be linear. A domain \(C\subset E\) is component-decomposable when
\[
C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m U_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\right\}.
\]
Consequently, for every \(c\in E^*\),
\[
\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m\min_{z_i\in C_i}\langle U_i^*c,z_i\rangle,
\]
and any collection of component minimizers \(z_i^*\) yields a global minimizer \(x^*=\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is decomposable when it is a linear image of component domains; its linear minimization problem then separates into independent component problems.
assumptions_latex: \(E,E_1,\ldots,E_m\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
Each \(C_i\) is nonempty and compact.
Each \(U_i:E_i\to E\) is linear.

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the component embedding or linear map.
Dual space of the ambient space.

children.title: Componentwise Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces exploiting independent or selectively accessible components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact assembly of component LMO gaps into the global Frank-Wolfe gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\right\},\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^mU_i x_i,
\]
and choose \(s_i\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z_i\in C_i}\langle U_i^*g,z_i\rangle\). Define
\[
G_C(x;g)=\max_{y\in C}\langle g,x-y\rangle,
\qquad G_i(x_i;U_i^*g)=\langle U_i^*g,x_i-s_i\rangle.
\]
Then \(G_C(x;g)=\sum_{i=1}^mG_i(x_i;U_i^*g)\). If \(g=\nabla f(x)\) for differentiable convex \(f\), this sum is the global Frank-Wolfe gap and satisfies \(f(x)-\min_{y\in C}f(y)\leq G_C(x;\nabla f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed component representation of the current point, component LMO gaps sum exactly to the global Frank-Wolfe gap.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\}\) with nonempty compact component sets.
\(x=\sum_{i=1}^mU_i x_i\) is a fixed component representation.
Each \(s_i\) minimizes \(\langle U_i^*g,z_i\rangle\) over \(C_i\).

notation.meaning: component linearization gap for the fixed representation

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Gap Aggregation
Componentwise Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear minimization over a linearly decomposed compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(c\in E^*\) and a representation \(C=\{\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\}\), query each component linear-minimization oracle with \(U_i^*c\) to obtain
\[
z_i^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z_i\in C_i}\langle U_i^*c,z_i\rangle.
\]
Return \(s=\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i^*\). Then \(s\in C\) and
\[
s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.
\]
Thus one global oracle call is implemented by \(m\) independent component calls, which may be executed in parallel; an approximate component solution with additive error \(\varepsilon_i\) gives aggregate error at most \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query every component with the transformed linear objective and combine the returned minimizers; component additive errors sum in the resulting global oracle answer.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{\sum_{i=1}^mU_i z_i:z_i\in C_i\}\) with nonempty compact components.
A linear-minimization oracle is available for every \(C_i\).

notation.meaning: Linear-minimizing point returned by component oracle i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variational comparison and output multiplicity of the two feasible-set interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), the Euclidean projection \(p=P_C(y)\) is the unique point satisfying \[\langle y-p,z-p\rangle\le0\qquad(\forall z\in C),\] equivalently \(y-p\in N_C(p)\). If the linear minimum is attained, then \[s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\langle c,z-s\rangle\ge0\qquad(\forall z\in C),\] equivalently \(-c\in N_C(s)\). Projection is single-valued, whereas linear minimization may return any point of an exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is uniquely characterized by its displacement normal, while linear minimization is characterized by the query normal and can expose an entire face.

review_flags: The displayed bound starts after the first Frank-Wolfe update; an initial objective gap cannot be bounded by diameter alone when y is arbitrarily far from C.
The reduction provides no uniform finite-call guarantee of exact projection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative many-call reduction from Euclidean projection to linear-minimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), set \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2\), and apply Frank-Wolfe over \(C\) using exact linear minimization. With exact line search or \(\gamma_j=2/(j+2)\), if \(p=P_C(y)\), then for \(k\geq1\), \[\phi(x_k)-\phi(p)\leq\frac{2D^2}{k+2},\qquad \|x_k-p\|_2\leq\frac{2D}{\sqrt{k+2}}.\] Consequently, distance accuracy \(\eta>0\) is obtained using \(O(D^2/\eta^2)\) linear-minimization calls. This is an approximate many-call simulation, not an exact one-call identification of the interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Running Frank-Wolfe on the squared-distance objective approximates Euclidean projection using repeated linear-minimization calls, with order D-squared over eta-squared calls for distance accuracy eta.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Projection by Repeated Linear Minimization
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Projection by Repeated Linear Minimization
Linear Minimization versus Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the Euclidean feasible-set interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), a projection oracle maps \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) to
\[
P_C(y)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2,
\]
whereas a linear-minimization oracle maps \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) to
\[
s_C(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.
\]
Projection balances a quadratic distance against all feasible points and requires only closedness; exact linear minimizers are guaranteed when \(C\) is additionally compact. Conditional-gradient methods use \(s_C(\nabla f(x))\), while projected-gradient methods use \(P_C(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\); the two interfaces need not have comparable implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection minimizes distance to a query point, while linear minimization exposes a supporting point. Conditional gradient uses the latter; projected gradient uses the former.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Compactness is imposed when existence of every linear minimizer is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(y)\) solves a quadratic problem, whereas \(s_C(c)\) solves a linear problem over the same feasible set.

children.title: Linear-Optimization Access
children.top_down_role: Computational access through linear objective optimization over the feasible region.

assumptions_latex: The queried linear minima are attained.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_{x\in C}\langle\lambda c,x\rangle=\arg\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\), while the response set for \(c=0\) is all of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale invariance and the degenerate zero-query boundary of point-valued linear-optimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle\lambda c,x\rangle=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle,\qquad \min_{x\in C}\langle\lambda c,x\rangle=\lambda\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.\] Thus an exact point-valued response depends only on the positive ray generated by a nonzero query. At \(c=0\), every point of \(C\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling preserves the optimizer set, while a zero query permits every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Zero-Query Degeneracy

assumptions_latex: \(s\in C\).
\(\ell\) is an independently valid lower bound on \(\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\).
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on the queried linear optimum

review_flags: A point-valued response without an independently valid lower bound does not by itself make the claimed additive error observable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable certificate for an additively approximate point-valued linear-optimization response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a query \(c\), a feasible point \(s\in C\) and scalar \(\ell\) form a certified additive \(\varepsilon\)-response if \[\ell\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle,\qquad \langle c,s\rangle-\ell\leq\varepsilon.\] These inequalities certify \(\langle c,s\rangle\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible response is certifiably additive-epsilon optimal when it is accompanied by a valid lower bound whose gap to the returned objective value is at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Additive Linear-Optimization Response

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-scaled additive approximation for point-valued linear-optimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) on query vectors. For nonempty compact \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), a scale-equivariant additive \(\varepsilon\)-linear-optimization oracle returns \(s_\varepsilon(c)\in C\) satisfying \[\langle c,s_\varepsilon(c)\rangle\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon\|c\|_*.\] This convention is invariant under \(c\mapsto\lambda c\) for \(\lambda>0\). For \(\varepsilon=0\) it is exact; at \(c=0\), every feasible point qualifies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling the allowed error by the query norm produces a point-valued approximation convention invariant under positive rescaling of the linear objective.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and compact}.
\varepsilon\geq0.
\|\cdot\|_*\text{ is the declared query norm}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle c,s_\varepsilon(c)\rangle\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon\|c\|_*\text{ is invariant under }c\mapsto\lambda c,\ \lambda>0.

notation.meaning: Declared norm used to scale query accuracy

review_flags: This convention differs from absolute additive error and general weak-optimization conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Equivariant Approximate Linear Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear optimum values depend only on the convex hull, while point-valued response sets retain representation information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty compact \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and query \(c\), \[\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle=\min_{x\in\operatorname{conv}C}\langle c,x\rangle.\] Thus linear-optimization values are invariant under convexification, although an oracle constrained to return a member of \(C\) differs from one allowed to return an arbitrary optimizer in \(\operatorname{conv}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying a compact feasible set leaves every linear optimum value unchanged but can alter the allowed point-valued responses.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and compact}.
c\in\mathbb R^n.
review_flags: The equality concerns optimum values, not equality of all point-valued response sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Invariance of Linear Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of exact linear-optimization responses over a compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. For \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(F_C(c):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\) is a nonempty compact exposed face of \(C\). It contains an extreme point of \(C\), so an exact point-valued oracle may select an extreme optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact linear minimizers form a compact exposed face containing at least one extreme point.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, compact, and convex}.
c\in\mathbb R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_C(c)\text{ is a nonempty compact exposed face containing an extreme point of }C.
review_flags: Extreme-point selection is existential; a particular oracle need not return an extreme optimizer.
At the zero query, the exposed face is the whole set.
knowledge_statements.title: Exposed-Face Response Set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-Only Access Does Not Return a Conditional-Gradient Atom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-type distinction between scalar linear-optimum access and point-valued linear-optimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value-only oracle for a query \(c\) returns only \(m_C(c):=\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\); it does not return an element of \(F_C(c):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\). For \(C=[-1,1]^2\) and \(c=(1,0)\), \(m_C(c)=-1\) while \(F_C(c)=\{-1\}\times[-1,1]\). Therefore the value-only interface supplies no optimizer selection unless an additional recovery procedure is provided.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar optimum-value response is not the point-valued atom required by a conditional-gradient update; optimizer recovery is an additional operation.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and compact}.
c\in\mathbb R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Value-only access does not by itself return an element of }F_C(c).
review_flags: The claim concerns the oracle output type; it does not rule out optimizer recovery using additional computation or access.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Only Access Does Not Return a Conditional-Gradient Atom

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for point-valued exact linear-optimization responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Point-valued exact linear-optimization access for every query requires each queried linear minimum to be finite and attained. Compactness is sufficient but not necessary. For \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(c=1\), \(\inf_{x\in C}cx=0\) is not attained. For \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(c=1\), the infimum is \(-\infty\). In either case no exact optimizing point can be returned for that query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without finiteness and attainment, an exact point-valued linear-optimization oracle may have no valid response.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
Exact access is required to return an optimizing point for the queried linear functional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\notin\mathbb R\ \text{or is not attained}\Longrightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle=\varnothing.
review_flags: Compactness is only a sufficient existence condition; the exact requirement is finite attainment for every admissible query.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment and Unboundedness Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Characterization of an Exact Linear-Optimization Response
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric optimality condition for an exact point-valued linear-optimization response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(s\in C\), and define \(N_C(s):=\{u:\langle u,x-s\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\). Then, for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \[s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -c\in N_C(s).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point minimizes a linear query exactly if and only if the negative query vector belongs to its normal cone.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
s\in C.
c\in\mathbb R^n.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone of C at s

review_flags: This is an exact mathematical characterization; verifying normal-cone membership may require additional access to the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Characterization of an Exact Linear-Optimization Response

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and absolute-additive point-valued linear optimization over a fixed compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. Exact linear-optimization access maps each \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) to some \(s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\). For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), absolute-additive \(\varepsilon\)-access returns \(s_\varepsilon(c)\in C\) such that \(\langle c,s_\varepsilon(c)\rangle\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon\). The response is an optimizing feasible point, not merely the optimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point-valued linear-optimization oracle returns a feasible linear minimizer, exactly or within a declared absolute additive error.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, compact, and convex}.
c\in\mathbb R^n.
\varepsilon\geq0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\ \text{or}\ \langle c,s_\varepsilon(c)\rangle\leq\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon.
review_flags: Absolute additive accuracy is not scale invariant; the accepted scale-equivariant convention is a distinct variant.
knowledge_statements.title: Point-Valued Linear-Optimization Access
Linear-Optimization Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and additive-accuracy linear optimization over a compact convex body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact. Exact linear-optimization access is an oracle that, for every query \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), returns
\[
s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.
\]
For \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), additive \(\varepsilon\)-accurate access instead returns \(s_\varepsilon(c)\in C\) satisfying
\[
\langle c,s_\varepsilon(c)\rangle\le \min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\varepsilon.
\]
The query exposes an optimizing feasible point, not merely the optimal value; this point-valued convention is the interface used by conditional-gradient updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-optimization access returns a feasible point minimizing a queried linear functional, exactly or within a specified additive objective error.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and compact.
The query vector \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) is represented in the chosen computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\), or its stated additive approximation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value representation associated with exact linear-optimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty compact set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), let \(\sigma_C(u)=\max_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\). Then \(\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle=-\sigma_C(-c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear minimization evaluates the negative support function in the opposite direction.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and compact}.
c\in\mathbb R^n.

children.title: Separation Access
children.top_down_role: Computational access through separating certificates for queried points.

assumptions_latex: \((a,\beta)\) is a valid strong separating certificate for \(y\) and \(C\).
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda a,\lambda\beta)\) remains valid and defines the same separating halfspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization freedom of strong separating certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\langle a,x\rangle\le\beta<\langle a,y\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\), then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\langle\lambda a,x\rangle\le\lambda\beta<\langle\lambda a,y\rangle\qquad(\forall x\in C).\] Thus a separating certificate is defined only up to positive scaling and may be normalized, for example by \(\|a\|_2=1\). A negative multiplier reverses the halfspace and is not equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating normal and offset may be multiplied by any positive scalar without changing the represented halfspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Scaling of Separation Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit Euclidean tolerance convention for weak separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(\delta>0\). A \(\delta\)-weak separation oracle, queried at \(y\), either certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(y,C)\le\delta\), or returns \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(\|a\|_2=1\) such that \[\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\le \langle a,y\rangle-\delta.\] The second output implies \(\operatorname{dist}(y,C)\ge\delta\). When \(\operatorname{dist}(y,C)=\delta\), either output is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weak oracle either certifies proximity within delta or returns a unit-normal separator having margin delta.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\delta>0\), with Euclidean distance and normalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Tolerant Weak Separation Access
Separation Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation access for a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A strong separation oracle accepts \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) and either certifies \(y\in C\), or returns \((a,\beta)\in(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\langle a,x\rangle\le\beta<\langle a,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
The returned inequality is directly verifiable as a claimed separating halfspace when support-function evaluation is available. Weak separation replaces exact membership and strict separation by explicitly prescribed distance or inequality tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle either confirms membership or returns a hyperplane whose closed feasible halfspace contains the entire set but excludes the query point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Queries use the same inner product as the separating inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(y\in C\), or \(\langle a,x\rangle\le\beta<\langle a,y\rangle\) for all \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: Nonzero normal of the separating hyperplane.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-separation definition fits the leaf, but it has no source. The final weak-separation sentence does not specify an actual tolerance convention and requires a source defining the intended weak oracle.

children.title: Oracle-Reduction Directions
children.top_down_role: Transformations transferring computational access between optimization-type plus separation-type interfaces.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
The queried linear minimum is attained at \(s\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct one-call transformation from a linear optimizer to a supporting halfspace with the prescribed normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\), then \[\langle c,x\rangle\ge\langle c,s\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Thus one point-valued linear-optimization call produces a supporting halfspace containing \(C\). This supplies support in the prescribed normal direction; by itself it is not a separation oracle for an arbitrary query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear minimizer supplies a supporting halfspace normal to the queried objective, but not necessarily a separator for an arbitrary external point.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Produces a Supporting Halfspace
Oracle-Reduction Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial equivalence of weak optimization and weak separation for well-bounded convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body with known rational data \(a_0\in\mathbb Q^n\) and \(0<r\le R\) satisfying
\[
B_2(a_0,r)\subseteq C\subseteq B_2(a_0,R).
\]
In the rational bit model, weak linear optimization over \(C\) and weak separation for \(C\) are polynomial-time Turing reducible to one another. More precisely, either oracle, queried to polynomially many bits of accuracy, implements the other using a number of calls and arithmetic operations polynomial in \(n\), the input encoding length, \(\log(R/r)\), and the requested output accuracy. The reduction is an approximate, well-bounded oracle equivalence and does not assert constant-call or exact-arithmetic equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rationally encoded, well-bounded convex body, weak linear optimization and weak separation simulate one another with polynomial overhead and controlled accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(B_2(a_0,r)\subseteq C\subseteq B_2(a_0,R)\) with known rational data.
Oracle queries and tolerances are rationally encoded.
Complexity is measured in the rational bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak optimization over \(C\) and weak separation for \(C\) are polynomial-time Turing interreducible.

notation.meaning: Closed Euclidean ball centered at a₀ with radius r.
Geometric conditioning ratio entering the reduction cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the correct role for oracle-reduction directions, but polynomial interreducibility depends on exact weak-optimization, weak-separation, encoding, and accuracy conventions. Those conventions and the complexity bound cannot be verified without a specific theorem locator.

children.title: Non-Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where reductions lose efficiency, precision, or structural compatibility.

assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The oracle guarantees only additive objective error and supplies no exact lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An additive \(\varepsilon\)-oracle need not return the exact minimizer, even when it is unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation of arbitrarily accurate additive access from exact access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(C=[0,\varepsilon]\) and query \(c=1\). The unique exact minimizer is \(0\), but the point \(s=\varepsilon\) satisfies \[cs=\min_{x\in C}cx+\varepsilon.\] Hence additive \(\varepsilon\)-accurate access cannot uniformly be identified with exact point-valued optimization, however small the positive tolerance is.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive additive tolerance there is an interval on which a legal approximate response differs from the unique exact minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Additive Accuracy Does Not Imply Exactness
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Additive Accuracy Does Not Imply Exactness

assumptions_latex: The oracle returns only the optimal scalar value.
No optimizer-selection rule or additional representation access is included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Value-only access does not fulfill the point-valued linear-optimization contract.

notation.meaning: Optimal scalar value for query c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-contract boundary between evaluating an optimum and returning an optimizing feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value oracle returning only \(v_C(c)=\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\) does not by its output contract provide a point-valued linear-optimization response. For \(C=[-1,1]^2\) and \(c=(1,0)\), the value is \(-1\), while the optimizer set is the entire edge \(\{-1\}\times[-1,1]\). Selecting a point from that face requires additional access or representation assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal scalar value does not itself return an optimizing point when the optimal face contains many points.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-Only and Point-Valued Access Are Distinct
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Only and Point-Valued Access Are Distinct

assumptions_latex: \(C=[-1,1]\times\{0\}\) is first viewed in \(\mathbb R^2\) and then in its affine hull.
Inner radius is measured using Euclidean balls in the declared space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No ambient ball of positive radius is contained in \(C\), while \(C\) has relative inner radius one in \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\).

notation.meaning: affine hull of the planar segment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit lower-dimensional set excluded by ambient well-boundedness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[-1,1]\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\). Then \(C\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, but for every \(a\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(r>0\), \(B_2(a,r)\nsubseteq C\). Thus any optimization-separation reduction requiring an ambient inclusion \(B_2(a,r)\subseteq C\) with \(r>0\) is inapplicable. After restricting the model to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), the same set has relative inner radius one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line segment in the plane has no positive ambient inner radius but is well bounded in its affine hull, so an ambient-space reduction hypothesis can fail solely because of dimension mismatch.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Inner-Radius Failure

assumptions_latex: Complexity is intended in a finite rational bit model.
No polynomial encoding-length bound is supplied for oracle queries, tolerances, or returned answers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding and precision boundary for optimization-separation correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction using polynomially many real-arithmetic oracle calls does not imply polynomial bit complexity unless query points, separating normals, objective coefficients, tolerances, and oracle answers have polynomially controlled finite encodings. Without those conditions, one nominal transaction may require arbitrarily many bits, and accuracy conversion may dominate the oracle-call count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial oracle-call overhead is not a polynomial-time bit guarantee unless every query, answer, and tolerance has controlled finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle-Call Equivalence Does Not Imply Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Equivalence Does Not Imply Bit Complexity
Non-Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of transferring polynomial weak-oracle equivalence to other models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial correspondence between optimization and separation is not an unconditional identity of oracle interfaces. Its standard reduction guarantee does not apply when the body lacks a supplied inner-radius bound, when \(C\) is lower-dimensional in the declared ambient space, when inputs have no finite encoding, or when exact strong answers replace tolerance-controlled weak answers. In particular, if \(C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\) has empty interior, then no \(r>0\) and \(a_0\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(B_2(a_0,r)\subseteq C\); hence the usual complexity bound involving \(\log(R/r)\) is undefined. Separate reductions or a restriction to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\) are then required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-oracle polynomial equivalence requires encoding, tolerances, and geometric bounds; lower-dimensional or exact-oracle settings fall outside that guarantee unless reformulated.
assumptions_latex: The referenced reduction requires a known positive inner radius and finite rational encoding.
The ambient space is the one used to define Euclidean balls and oracle tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}(C)=\varnothing\), the standard well-bounded reduction hypothesis \(B_2(a_0,r)\subseteq C\) with \(r>0\) fails.

notation.meaning: Affine hull of the feasible set.
Interior in the declared ambient Euclidean space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empty-interior observation is correct in the declared ambient space and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind. The broader claims about when optimization-separation reductions cease to apply depend on a particular oracle theorem and require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Oracle Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Cost models separating objective, gradient, linear-oracle, and representation work.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-dependent refinement of separated oracle accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the \(t\)-th call to resource \(j\) is requested at tolerance \(\eta_{j,t}>0\) and costs \(c_j(\eta_{j,t})\), define \[W_j=\sum_{t=1}^{N_j}c_j(\eta_{j,t}),\qquad W=\sum_jW_j.\] A unit-call model is the specialization \(c_j\equiv w_j\). Thus a bound on \(N_j\) alone need not bound total work when \(c_j(\eta)\) grows as \(\eta\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For inexact oracles, modeled work sums tolerance-dependent call costs; fixed unit costs are a specialization.
assumptions_latex: Every inexact call declares its requested tolerance.
Each comparison uses a consistent accuracy and cost convention.

notation.meaning: Accuracy requested from call t of resource j.
Modeled cost of a resource-j call at tolerance eta.

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Dependent Oracle Work

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Counts Do Not Determine Runtime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between abstract call complexity and implementation work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separated count vector \((N_j)_j\) does not by itself determine arithmetic work or elapsed time: implementations with identical counts may have different per-call accuracy costs, representation sizes, memory costs, or parallel schedules. A scalar comparison \(\sum_jw_jN_j\) is meaningful only after common weights, accuracies, and work-versus-depth conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal oracle counts need not mean equal runtime; scalar comparisons require a shared cost, accuracy, and parallelism convention.
assumptions_latex: Counts use the same declared oracle interfaces.
No uniform implementation cost is inferred unless supplied by the model.

notation.meaning: Declared unit cost for category j.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Counts Do Not Determine Runtime
Oracle Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separated accounting for conditional-gradient computational resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an algorithmic run, let \(N_f,N_{\nabla f},N_{\mathrm{LMO}},N_{\mathrm{rep}}\) denote respectively the numbers of objective evaluations, gradient evaluations, linear-minimization calls, and representation-update operations. A separated oracle-cost model reports the vector
\[
\mathcal C=(N_f,N_{\nabla f},N_{\mathrm{LMO}},N_{\mathrm{rep}})
\]
rather than identifying iteration count with total work. Given nonnegative implementation-dependent unit costs \(w_f,w_{\nabla f},w_{\mathrm{LMO}},w_{\mathrm{rep}}\), the associated scalar work estimate is
\[
W=w_fN_f+w_{\nabla f}N_{\nabla f}+w_{\mathrm{LMO}}N_{\mathrm{LMO}}+w_{\mathrm{rep}}N_{\mathrm{rep}}.
\]
Parallel component calls may additionally be charged by total work or critical-path depth, which must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle cost is recorded separately for objective, gradient, linear-minimization, and representation work, with optional implementation-dependent weights or parallel-depth accounting.
assumptions_latex: Every charged operation belongs to a declared oracle or representation category.
Unit costs are nonnegative and fixed for the reported scalar estimate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separated accounting convention matches the leaf and definition is a suitable content kind, but the selected resource categories, weighted model, and parallel-depth convention have no cited support or explicit standard-field rationale.
