children.title: Generalized Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gap-based certificates induced by structured local models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Structured-Oracle Values Need an Error Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for gaps formed from approximate generalized-oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_x(v)=\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle+h(v)\), let \(\widetilde v\) be an inexact oracle output, and set \(\widetilde g(x)=m_x(x)-m_x(\widetilde v)\). In general \(\widetilde g(x)\le g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x)\) and need not upper-bound primal error. If \(m_x(\widetilde v)\le\inf_vm_x(v)+\delta\), then \(\widetilde g(x)+\delta\) is a valid upper certificate. Without such control, \(f(t)=t\), \(h=\iota_{[-1,1]}\), \(x=1\), and \(\widetilde v=x\) give \(\widetilde g(x)=0\) while the primal error is \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncontrolled approximate structured-oracle point can underestimate primal error; a certified additive oracle-value error repairs the certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex, \(h\) is proper closed convex, and \(h(x)<\infty\).
For the repaired certificate, a valid additive model-value error \(\delta\ge0\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi(x)-\Phi_*\le g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x)\le\widetilde g(x)+\delta;\quad\delta\text{ is essential in general.}
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Structured-Oracle Values Need an Error Certificate
Generalized Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable generalized conditional-gradient gap for smooth-plus-structured convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\Phi=f+h\), let
\[
v(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v}
\{\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle+h(v)\}
\]
and define
\[
g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x):=
\langle\nabla f(x),x-v(x)\rangle+h(x)-h(v(x)).
\]
For every minimizer \(x_*\) of \(\Phi\), convexity of \(f\) gives
\[
0\leq \Phi(x)-\Phi(x_*)\leq g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x).
\]
Hence \(g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-suboptimality. Moreover, \(g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\) when the oracle minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized conditional-gradient gap is nonnegative, upper-bounds primal suboptimality, and vanishes exactly at first-order optimal points under oracle attainment.
assumptions_latex: f is differentiable and convex, and h is proper closed convex.
The generalized oracle minimum at x is attained.
A minimizer x_* of f+h exists.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized gap is correctly formed, upper-bounds composite primal suboptimality, and vanishes exactly when x itself solves the linearized structured oracle, equivalently satisfying the stated first-order inclusion. Its certificate content kind is exact, but the record has no inspectable source.

children.title: Primal-Dual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates relating primal progress to an associated dual representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal-dual gap specialized to the gradient-generated dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal problem \(\inf_x\{f(x)+h(x)\}\), the Fenchel dual is
\[
\sup_y\{-f^*(-y)-h^*(y)\}.
\]
Every primal-dual pair \((x,y)\) has certificate
\[
G(x,y):=f(x)+h(x)+f^*(-y)+h^*(y)\geq0,
\]
and weak duality yields \(\Phi(x)-\Phi_*\leq G(x,y)\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then choosing \(y=-\nabla f(x)\) gives
\[
G(x,-\nabla f(x))=
\langle\nabla f(x),x\rangle+h(x)+h^*(-\nabla f(x)).
\]
This value is computable whenever the structured oracle supplies the corresponding conjugate value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel weak duality supplies a primal-dual gap bounding primal error; the negative gradient gives a canonical dual point for generalized conditional gradient.
assumptions_latex: f and h are proper closed convex functions with a finite primal optimum.
f is differentiable at the queried primal point x.
The displayed conjugate values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi(x)-\Phi_*\leq G(x,y); in particular y=-\nabla f(x) yields the canonical gradient-generated certificate.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugates of f and h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Fenchel Gap Characterizes Primal-Dual Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality conditions encoded by the composite Fenchel certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(G(x,y)=f(x)+h(x)+f^*(-y)+h^*(y)\), \[G(x,y)=0\iff -y\in\partial f(x)\ \text{and}\ y\in\partial h(x).\] Such a pair satisfies \(0\in\partial f(x)+\partial h(x)\) and attains equal primal and dual values. If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the first inclusion forces \(y=-\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel gap vanishes exactly when both Fenchel–Young equality conditions hold, yielding primal-dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions.
All displayed values are finite at \((x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of generalized and canonical Fenchel gaps, and dominance of an optimized dual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the generalized oracle at \(x\) is attained at \(v(x)\). Fenchel conjugacy gives
\[
h^*(-\nabla f(x))=-\langle\nabla f(x),v(x)\rangle-h(v(x)),
\]
so the generalized gap and canonical Fenchel certificate coincide:
\[
g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x)=G(x,-\nabla f(x)).
\]
If \(Y\) is any dual search set containing \(-\nabla f(x)\), then
\[
\inf_{y\in Y}G(x,y)\leq g_{\mathrm{GCG}}(x).
\]
Thus optimizing the dual point can only strengthen the numerical upper bound, while both certificates remain valid upper bounds on primal suboptimality whenever finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized gap equals the Fenchel gap at the negative gradient; minimizing the Fenchel gap over a larger dual set can only produce a tighter certificate.
assumptions_latex: The generalized structured oracle at x is attained.
f is differentiable at x, and f and h are proper closed convex.
The dual search set Y contains -\nabla f(x).

notation.meaning: candidate set of dual certificate points

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Numerical Certificate Dominance Does Not Imply Computational Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computability boundary for optimizing the Fenchel certificate over a dual search set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although \(\inf_{y\in Y}G(x,y)\le G(x,-\nabla f(x))\) when \(-\nabla f(x)\in Y\), this compares certificate values only. Computing the infimum may require an additional dual optimization or conjugate evaluations unavailable from the generalized conditional-gradient oracle. No oracle-cost or runtime dominance follows without a procedure and complexity bound for producing the optimized certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimized dual gap is numerically no weaker than the canonical generalized gap but may be more expensive or unavailable to compute.
assumptions_latex: \(-\nabla f(x)\in Y\).
The compared certificate values are well-defined.

notation.meaning: Dual search set containing the canonical dual point.
Declared cost of evaluating a certificate.

Then f(x)-\min_{y\in C_\delta}f(y)\leq\langle\nabla f(x),x-\tilde s(x)\rangle. Thus a contracted gap at most \varepsilon certifies \varepsilon-suboptimality for the contracted problem, not necessarily for minimization over C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Contraction Can Exclude the Original Optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact contracted optimization from original-domain accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=[0,1], u_0=1, \delta\in(0,1), and f(x)=x. Then C_\delta=[\delta,1], the original minimizer is 0, and the contracted optimum is \delta. Hence an exact solution of the fixed contracted problem has original-domain objective error \delta>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed positive contraction can permanently exclude a boundary optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Contraction Can Exclude the Original Optimum
Fixed-Contraction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frank–Wolfe applied to a prescribed contraction of a compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a compact convex set \(C\), an anchor \(u_0\in C\), and fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), define
\[
C_\delta:=(1-\delta)C+\delta u_0.
\]
Initialize \(x_0\in C_\delta\). At iteration \(t\), compute
\[
s_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x_t),s\rangle,
\qquad
\tilde s_t=(1-\delta)s_t+\delta u_0,
\]
choose \(\gamma_t\in[0,1]\) by a prescribed Frank–Wolfe stepsize rule, and set
\[
x_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)x_t+\gamma_t\tilde s_t.
\]
Stop when \(\langle\nabla f(x_t),x_t-\tilde s_t\rangle\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(x_t\), which remains in \(C_\delta\) throughout.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-contraction method runs Frank–Wolfe on a domain contracted toward a fixed anchor, transforming each original-domain oracle atom before updating.
assumptions_latex: C is nonempty, compact, and convex, with anchor u_0\in C.
f is differentiable on a neighborhood of C_\delta.
The linear minimization oracle over C is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_t\in C_\delta for all t, and the transformed atom \tilde s_t minimizes the same linearization over C_\delta.

notation.meaning: domain C contracted toward u_0 by factor \delta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transformed atom does minimize the linearization over the contracted domain, and convex-combination invariance keeps all iterates in that domain. The algorithm fits the Fixed-Contraction Methods container, but no source is provided. Moreover, if the stopping test is intended to certify epsilon-suboptimality rather than merely define termination, convexity of f must be assumed and sourced.

Hence decreasing the contraction parameter preserves feasibility of the current point; increasing it may exclude that point and requires explicit feasibility restoration.

Adaptive-Contraction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive Frank–Wolfe iteration over contractions centered at a relative-interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be compact and convex, choose \(u\in\operatorname{relint}C\), and initialize \(x_0\in C_{\delta_0}:=(1-\delta_0)C+\delta_0u\). At iteration \(k\), select \(\delta_k\in(0,1]\) from the observed objective values, gradients, or conditional-gradient gaps, subject to \(x_k\in C_{\delta_k}\). Compute \(v_k\in\arg\min_{v\in C}\langle\nabla f(x_k),v\rangle\), set \(s_k=(1-\delta_k)v_k+\delta_ku\), choose \(\gamma_k\in[0,1]\), and update \(x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_k+\gamma_ks_k\). Stop when the contracted gap \(\langle\nabla f(x_k),x_k-s_k\rangle\) meets the prescribed tolerance; otherwise adapt \(\delta_{k+1}\) and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method adaptively changes a feasible-set contraction, solves each contracted linear oracle through the original domain, and takes a feasible conditional-gradient step.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional vector space.
\(u\in\operatorname{relint}C\) and \(f\) is differentiable on every contraction used.
The contraction rule preserves \(x_k\in C_{\delta_k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in C_{\delta_k}\subseteq C\), and each contracted oracle requires one linear minimization over \(C\).

notation.meaning: Fixed contraction center in the relative interior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes cyclic Gauss–Seidel-style block oracles from parallel block oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Block i in a cyclic sweep uses \nabla_i f(x^{t,i-1}) after earlier blocks have changed. Unless the relevant cross-block gradient components are invariant under those changes, replacing these gradients by \nabla_i f(x^t) changes the oracle atoms and generally the resulting iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Within-Sweep Block Gaps Are Not an Aggregate Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies stopping certificates for sequentially refreshed cyclic sweeps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a cyclic sweep, block i is queried at x^{t,i-1}. Consequently, the sum of the resulting quantities \langle\nabla_i f(x^{t,i-1}),x_i^{t,i-1}-s_i^t\rangle generally is not the full Frank–Wolfe gap at any single iterate. A full product-domain certificate at a sweep endpoint requires all block gaps to be evaluated or validly bounded at that common endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block gaps gathered at different intermediate cyclic iterates cannot generally be summed into one full-gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on a Cartesian-product domain.
Each cyclic block oracle uses the current partially updated iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-Curvature Descent Within a Cyclic Sweep
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step descent for a cyclic block conditional-gradient update at its refreshed intermediate iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At y=x^{t,i-1}, let s_i\in\arg\min_{s\in C_i}\langle\nabla_i f(y),s\rangle, d=P_i(s_i-y_i), and g_i(y)=-\langle\nabla f(y),d\rangle. If f(y+\gamma d)\le f(y)-\gamma g_i(y)+\tfrac{C_i}{2}\gamma^2 for every \gamma\in[0,1], then \gamma=\min\{g_i(y)/C_i,1\} gives f(y+\gamma d)\le f(y)-\tfrac12\min\{g_i(y)^2/C_i,g_i(y)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refreshed cyclic block update decreases the objective when its step is calibrated to a valid block-curvature bound.
assumptions_latex: f is differentiable on the product domain.
C_i>0 and the displayed block-curvature inequality holds.
The block linear oracle is exact.

At a sweep endpoint \(x^{t+1}\), compute \(s_i\in\arg\min_{s_i\in C_i}\langle
abla_i f(x^{t+1}),s_iangle\) and \(g_i=\langle
abla_i f(x^{t+1}),x_i^{t+1}-s_iangle\) for every block. Then \(g(x^{t+1})=\sum_{i=1}^m g_i=\max_{s\in C}\langle
abla f(x^{t+1}),x^{t+1}-sangle\). If \(f\) is convex and attains \(f^*\), then \(f(x^{t+1})-f^*\le g(x^{t+1})\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sweep-level descent obtained by summing refreshed block-curvature decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^{t,0}=x^t\) and suppose that, for every block \(i\), the cyclic update from \(x^{t,i-1}\) to \(x^{t,i}\) satisfies the block-curvature hypotheses with gap \(g_{t,i}\geq0\), curvature \(C_i>0\), and step \(\gamma_{t,i}=\min\{g_{t,i}/C_i,1\}\). Then \[f(x^{t+1})=f(x^{t,m})\leq f(x^t)-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m\min\left\{\frac{g_{t,i}^2}{C_i},g_{t,i}\right\}.\]

Cyclic Block Conditional Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential deterministic block Frank–Wolfe updates on a Cartesian-product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\) and initialize \(x^0\in C\). For each sweep \(t=0,1,\ldots\), set \(x^{t,0}=x^t\) and process blocks in the fixed order \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Compute \(s_i^t\in\arg\min_{s_i\in C_i}\langle\nabla_i f(x^{t,i-1}),s_i\rangle\), choose \(\gamma_{t,i}\in[0,1]\), set \(x_i^{t,i}=(1-\gamma_{t,i})x_i^{t,i-1}+\gamma_{t,i}s_i^t\), and set \(x_j^{t,i}=x_j^{t,i-1}\) for every \(j\ne i\). After the sweep, set \(x^{t+1}=x^{t,m}\). Stop according to the prescribed objective, block-gap, or iteration criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each sweep starts from the preceding sweep endpoint, visits every block in a fixed order, and immediately applies one feasible block conditional-gradient update.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f\) is differentiable on \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\).
Every stepsize \(\gamma_{t,i}\) belongs to \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every intermediate iterate belongs to \(C\), and one complete sweep makes exactly \(m\) block linear-oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Gradient component associated with block i.
Iterate after updating block i during sweep t.

children.title: Randomized Block Conditional Gradients
children.top_down_role: Randomized block-selection methods and their oracle-complexity family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the coverage requirement for full product-domain conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If block j has conditional selection probability zero at every iteration, the method never queries or updates it. Convergence of sampled gaps or updates then cannot imply g_j(x)=0 or full product-domain stationarity. Generic full-block conclusions require almost-sure infinite coverage, commonly ensured by uniformly positive conditional probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A never-sampled block can remain nonstationary, so every block requires persistent coverage.
assumptions_latex: Only sampled blocks are queried and updated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{k,j}=0\ \forall k\Rightarrow\text{ sampled convergence need not imply }g_j(x)=0\)

notation.meaning: conditional probability of selecting block j

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Block Coverage Is Necessary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates a serial random block oracle call to the aggregate gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For g_i(x):=\max_{s_i\in C_i}\langle\nabla_i f(x),x_i-s_i\rangle and conditional probabilities p_i>0, \mathbb E[g_I(x)\mid x]=\sum_i p_i g_i(x) and \mathbb E[g_I(x)/p_I\mid x]=\sum_i g_i(x)=g(x). Under uniform sampling, \mathbb E[g_I(x)\mid x]=g(x)/m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sampled block gap is probability-weighted, while inverse-probability scaling is an unbiased estimator of the full gap.
assumptions_latex: The distribution is conditional on the pre-draw history.
Each block linear oracle is exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Sampled Block Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance of the Inverse-Probability Full-Gap Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-moment identity governing serial randomized block-gap estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Conditionally on x, sample I with p_i>0 and set \widehat g=g_I(x)/p_I. Then \mathbb E[\widehat g\mid x]=g(x), \mathbb E[\widehat g^2\mid x]=\sum_i g_i(x)^2/p_i, and \operatorname{Var}(\widehat g\mid x)=\sum_i g_i(x)^2/p_i-g(x)^2. If all g_i(x)>0, the second moment is minimized over strictly positive probabilities by p_i=g_i(x)/g(x). If some gaps vanish, the same value is the infimum under p_i>0 and is attained only after allowing zero probability on zero-gap blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-probability gap estimates are unbiased, and their variance depends explicitly on the sampling probabilities; gap-proportional sampling is optimal subject to the stated support convention.
assumptions_latex: p_i>0 and \sum_i p_i=1.
Every g_i(x) is an exact nonnegative block Frank–Wolfe gap.

notation.meaning: Inverse-probability estimator of the full Frank–Wolfe gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance of the Inverse-Probability Full-Gap Estimator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Convex Rate for Fixed Positive Block Probabilities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective convergence for exact serial randomized block oracles under block curvature bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p_i>0, p_{\min}=\min_i p_i, and C_p=\sum_i p_iC_i. Suppose f(x+\gamma P_i(s_i-x_i))\le f(x)-\gamma g_i(x)+\tfrac{\gamma^2}{2}C_i for 0\le\gamma\le1. For h_k=\mathbb E[f(x^k)-f^*], independent fixed-probability sampling gives h_{k+1}\le(1-p_{\min}\gamma_k)h_k+\tfrac12C_p\gamma_k^2. With \gamma_k=2/[p_{\min}(k+2/p_{\min})], define A=\max\{(2/p_{\min})h_0,2C_p/p_{\min}^2\}; then h_K\le A/(K+2/p_{\min}). Each iteration uses one block linear-oracle call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed positive block probabilities and block curvature yield an explicit inverse-linear expected convex rate, with probability dependence through the least-sampled block and weighted curvature.
assumptions_latex: C=\prod_i C_i is compact and convex.
f is convex and differentiable and attains f^*.
Block i is sampled with fixed probability p_i>0 conditionally on the past.
Every selected block linear oracle is exact.
The displayed block-curvature inequality holds with constants C_i.

notation.meaning: Probability-weighted sum of block curvature constants.
Expected objective suboptimality after k sampled block updates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), initialize \(x^0\in C\), and fix probabilities \(p_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\). At iteration \(k\), independently sample \(I_k\) with \(\mathbb P(I_k=i)=p_i\), compute \(s_{I_k}^k\in\arg\min_{s\in C_{I_k}}\langle\nabla_{I_k}f(x^k),s\rangle\), and choose \(\gamma_k\in[0,1]\). Set \(x_{I_k}^{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_{I_k}^k+\gamma_ks_{I_k}^k\) and \(x_j^{k+1}=x_j^k\) for \(j\ne I_k\). Stop according to a prescribed randomized gap, objective, or iteration criterion and return the current feasible iterate.

\(f\) is differentiable on the product domain.
The sampling probabilities are positive and fixed independently of the current draw.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a condition converting simultaneous block gaps into descent.

Let d_i=s_i-x_i on selected blocks and d_i=0 otherwise. Suppose M>0 and f(x+\gamma d)\leq f(x)+\gamma\langle
abla f(x),dangle+ rac{M}{2}\gamma^2\lVert dVert^2 for 0\leq\gamma\leq1. With G_S(x):=-\langle
abla f(x),dangle, every 0<\gamma<\min\{1,2G_S(x)/(M\lVert dVert^2)\} gives strict descent when G_S(x)>0 and d
eq0.

The displayed joint curvature inequality holds with \(M>0\).

notation.meaning: sum of selected block Frank–Wolfe gaps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Block Gaps Do Not Justify an Unrestricted Simultaneous Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits interference through cross-block curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=[-1,1]^2, f(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+x_2)^2, and x=(1,1). Both block linear oracles return s_1=s_2=-1, and both block gaps equal 8. The simultaneous full step gives x^+=(-1,-1) and f(x^+)=f(x)=4.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually improving block atoms can produce no decrease when committed together with a full step.
assumptions_latex: Both block oracles use the common snapshot \(x=(1,1)\).
The simultaneous stepsize is \(\gamma=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Block Gaps Do Not Justify an Unrestricted Simultaneous Step

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Frank–Wolfe certification when every product block is queried from one synchronized iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i, let s_i(x)\in\arg\min_{s_i\in C_i}\langle
abla_i f(x),s_iangle and g_i(x)=\langle
abla_i f(x),x_i-s_i(x)angle. If all block oracles are evaluated at the same x, then g(x):=\max_{s\in C}\langle
abla f(x),x-sangle=\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x). If f is convex and attains f^* on C, then f(x)-f^*\le g(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common-snapshot calls on every block produce gaps whose sum is exactly the full Frank–Wolfe gap and, for convex objectives, certifies objective error.
assumptions_latex: C=\prod_i C_i, with each C_i nonempty and compact.
f is differentiable on C.
Every block gap is evaluated at the same iterate x.
The suboptimality conclusion additionally assumes convexity and attainment of f^*.

notation.meaning: Block-i Frank–Wolfe gap at the common snapshot.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Activation Parallel Blocks Equal a Product-Domain Frank–Wolfe Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence and oracle accounting for the synchronous variant that activates every block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When S_k=\{1,\ldots,m\}, the tuple s^k=(s_1^k,\ldots,s_m^k) belongs to \arg\min_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x^k),s\rangle, so the simultaneous update is x^{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x^k+\gamma_k s^k. If f is convex and satisfies f(x+\gamma(s-x))\le f(x)+\gamma\langle\nabla f(x),s-x\rangle+\tfrac{C_F}{2}\gamma^2, then with \gamma_k=2/(k+2), \mathbb E is unnecessary and f(x^k)-f^*\le 2C_F/(k+2) after the usual initialization-compatible bound. Each round uses m block-oracle calls with ideal oracle depth one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activating all blocks in parallel is exactly ordinary Frank–Wolfe on the product domain, giving the standard inverse-linear convex rate with parallel block-oracle depth one.
assumptions_latex: Every C_i is nonempty, compact, and convex.
f is convex and differentiable and attains f^*.
All m exact block oracles use the same x^k.
The displayed product-direction curvature inequality holds with C_F<\infty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^k)-f^*=O(C_F/k),\quad \text{with }m\text{ block calls and ideal oracle depth }1\text{ per round}.

notation.meaning: Frank–Wolfe curvature bound for full product-domain directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Activation Parallel Blocks Equal a Product-Domain Frank–Wolfe Step

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Selected-Block Gap Is Not a Full Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping limitation for a partially activated common-snapshot round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(G_S(x)=\sum_{i\in S}g_i(x)\). Generally \(G_S(x)=0\) does not imply \(g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x)=0\). For \(C=[-1,1]^2\), \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_2\), \(x=(0,1)\), and \(S=\{1\}\), one has \(G_S(x)=0\) but \(g(x)=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero gap over only the activated blocks cannot certify full stationarity.
assumptions_latex: Selected block gaps are evaluated at one common iterate.
The active set may omit a block.

notation.meaning: Sum of Frank–Wolfe gaps over the active blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Selected-Block Gap Is Not a Full Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activation-dependent rate for synchronized parallel blocks without cross-block objective coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i) on C=\prod_i C_i, with each f_i convex, differentiable, and of Frank--Wolfe curvature at most C_i^{\mathrm{FW}}. In synchronized round k choose S_k and update every i\in S_k concurrently from the common snapshot. Give block i stepsize 2/(r_i+2) on its r_i-th update. If n_i(K) counts its activations in the first K rounds and f_i(x_i^0)-f_i^*\le C_i^{\mathrm{FW}}, then f(x^K)-f^*\le\sum_i2C_i^{\mathrm{FW}}/(n_i(K)+2). The rounds use \sum_{k<K}|S_k| block-oracle calls and ideal oracle depth K.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a separable objective, partially activated synchronized blocks are independent Frank–Wolfe processes whose errors depend on their activation counts.
assumptions_latex: Every C_i is nonempty, compact, and convex.
f(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i), with each f_i convex and differentiable.
Selected blocks use one common snapshot and exact block oracles.
Each block uses its update-count stepsize and satisfies the stated initialization bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\) and \(x^0\in C\). At synchronized round \(k\), choose a nonempty set \(S_k\). From the same snapshot \(x^k\), compute concurrently \(s_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s_i\in C_i}\langle\nabla_i f(x^k),s_i\rangle\) for every \(i\in S_k\). After all selected responses are available, choose \(\gamma_k\in[0,1]\), set \(x_i^{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_i^k+\gamma_k s_i^k\) for \(i\in S_k\), and leave unselected blocks unchanged.

f\text{ is differentiable on }C.

children.top_down_role: Sliding methods for deterministic smooth convex optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Justifies termination of each projection-free quadratic-model subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable convex inner model q_k on compact convex X, define G_k(z):=\max_{v\in X}\langle\nabla q_k(z),z-v\rangle. Then q_k(z)-\min_{v\in X}q_k(v)\leq G_k(z). Thus G_k(z_k)\leq\eta_k certifies an \eta_k-suboptimal inner solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner Frank–Wolfe gap certifies the required accuracy of the quadratic-model solve.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(q_k\) is differentiable and convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Conditional-Gradient Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncontrolled Inner Error Breaks the Sliding Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why the inner tolerance schedule is part of the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When an accelerated outer recurrence replaces an exact model minimizer by z_k, its estimate contains an inexactness contribution controlled by q_k(z_k)-\min_Xq_k. Performing an unspecified fixed number of inner linear-oracle steps does not ensure the required estimate. A convergence theorem therefore needs a quantitative condition on the weighted accumulation of inner errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary truncation of the inner loop need not preserve the accelerated outer guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The outer analysis uses approximate minimization of \(q_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{outer acceleration requires a declared accumulated-inner-error bound}\)

notation.meaning: certified error of the kth inner solve

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Inner Error Breaks the Sliding Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Gap Controls Distance to the Quadratic-Model Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens the inner stopping certificate for the strongly convex sliding subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let q_k(z)=\langle g_k,z\rangle+\tfrac{\beta_k}{2}\|z-z_{k-1}\|^2 on a nonempty compact convex set X, let z_k^*\in\arg\min_Xq_k, and define G_k(z)=\max_{v\in X}\langle\nabla q_k(z),z-v\rangle. Then \tfrac{\beta_k}{2}\|z-z_k^*\|^2\le q_k(z)-q_k(z_k^*)\le G_k(z). Consequently, G_k(z)\le\eta_k implies \|z-z_k^*\|\le\sqrt{2\eta_k/\beta_k}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner Frank–Wolfe gap bounds both quadratic-model suboptimality and distance to the exact inner minimizer.
assumptions_latex: X is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\beta_k>0.
The norm is induced by the quadratic model's inner product.

notation.meaning: Exact minimizer of the kth inner quadratic model.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner Gap Controls Distance to the Quadratic-Model Minimizer
Deterministic Conditional-Gradient Sliding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accelerated outer gradient steps with inner projection-free quadratic-model solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact and convex, choose \(x_0=z_0\in X\), and prescribe sequences \(\gamma_k\in(0,1]\), \(\beta_k>0\), and \(\eta_k\ge0\). For \(k=1,2,\ldots\), form \(y_k=(1-\gamma_k)x_{k-1}+\gamma_k z_{k-1}\) and evaluate \(g_k=\nabla f(y_k)\) once. Using only linear minimization over \(X\), find \(z_k\in X\) whose conditional-gradient gap for \(q_k(z)=\langle g_k,z\rangle+\frac{\beta_k}{2}\lVert z-z_{k-1}\rVert^2\) is at most \(\eta_k\). Set \(x_k=(1-\gamma_k)x_{k-1}+\gamma_kz_k\). Stop at the prescribed outer index and output \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional-gradient sliding reuses one outer gradient evaluation while an inner Frank–Wolfe loop approximately minimizes a strongly convex quadratic model.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, compact, and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(f\) is convex, differentiable, and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient on \(X\).
The inner gap tolerance satisfies \(\eta_k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each outer iteration evaluates \(\nabla f\) once, while all additional inner work consists of linear-oracle calls over \(X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth-convex gradient complexity of conditional-gradient sliding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth on a compact convex set \(X\) of diameter \(D\), and let \(f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). For the standard accelerated deterministic conditional-gradient sliding schedule, an iterate \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) can be produced using \[N_{\nabla}(\varepsilon)=O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{LD^2}{\varepsilon}}\right)\] evaluations of the full gradient. The count treats one exact evaluation of \(\nabla f\) as one gradient-oracle call and excludes the linear minimizations performed by the inner conditional-gradient procedures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth convex minimization, deterministic conditional-gradient sliding attains epsilon accuracy with order square-root inverse-epsilon full-gradient evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(X\).
\(X\) is compact, convex, and has diameter \(D\).
Accuracy means \(f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon>0\).

notation.meaning: Diameter of the feasible set in the smoothness norm.
Minimum objective value over the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-minimization complexity accompanying deterministic conditional-gradient sliding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the smooth convex setting and the standard inner-tolerance schedule of deterministic conditional-gradient sliding, an iterate \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) can be obtained with \[N_{\mathrm{LMO}}(\varepsilon)=O\!\left(\frac{LD^2}{\varepsilon}\right)\] calls to a linear minimization oracle returning an element of \(\arg\min_{s\in X}\langle c,s\rangle\) for a supplied covector \(c\). This count aggregates every inner conditional-gradient call across all outer iterations and does not count full-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional-gradient sliding uses order inverse-epsilon linear-minimization calls for smooth convex epsilon accuracy, counting all inner oracle work.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth on the compact convex set \(X\).
The diameter of \(X\) is \(D\).
The deterministic sliding method uses its standard accuracy-dependent inner stopping schedule.

notation.meaning: Covector supplied to the linear oracle.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard smooth-convex conditional-gradient sliding rate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-oracle complexity claim has the correct role, but no source identifies the inner tolerance schedule or theorem yielding the aggregate inverse-epsilon bound.

children.title: Complexity-Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where gradient cost scales differently from linear-oracle cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic separation between the stated gradient and linear-oracle upper-bound scales at high accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(L>0\) and \(D>0\), and let \(\varepsilon/(LD^2)\to0\). Define the benchmark scales \(U_{\nabla}(\varepsilon)=\sqrt{LD^2/\varepsilon}\) and \(U_{\mathrm{LMO}}(\varepsilon)=LD^2/\varepsilon\). Then \[\frac{U_{\mathrm{LMO}}(\varepsilon)}{U_{\nabla}(\varepsilon)}=\sqrt{\frac{LD^2}{\varepsilon}}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Thus the commonly stated conditional-gradient-sliding upper-bound scales permit a smaller order for full-gradient evaluations than for linear-oracle calls. This comparison does not by itself assert that the actual oracle counts, or their optimal complexities, have this ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At high accuracy, the stated linear-oracle upper-bound scale exceeds the stated gradient upper-bound scale by a growing square-root factor; this does not determine the ratio of actual counts.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(D\) are fixed and positive.
\(\varepsilon/(LD^2)\to0\).
The two benchmark bounds use the same problem class and accuracy convention.

notation.meaning: Benchmark scale for the full-gradient upper bound.
Benchmark scale for the linear-oracle upper bound.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic comparison of CGS oracle-bound scales

children.title: Evaluation-Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between first-order computation plus linear-oracle usage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Bounds Do Not Establish a Joint Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on inferring a jointly achievable oracle pair from separate marginal bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The assertions \(\exists(a,b)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon:a\le G\) and \(\exists(c,d)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon:d\le M\) do not imply \(\exists(u,v)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon:u\le G,\ v\le M\). The set \(\{(1,100),(100,1)\}\) with \(G=M=1\) is a counterexample. A claimed joint pair must be attained by one schedule or by a proved schedule-combination construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate good gradient and LMO bounds need not be jointly achievable by one schedule.
assumptions_latex: All pairs use the same problem class, accuracy criterion, and oracle-accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Bounds Do Not Establish a Joint Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Scalarization and Unsupported Frontier Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between positive weighted oracle costs and Pareto-minimal evaluation pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha,\beta>0\), every attained minimizer of \(\alpha u+\beta v\) over \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) is Pareto minimal. The converse can fail for a discrete nonconvex achievable set: all points of \(\{(0,3),(2,2),(3,0)\}\) are Pareto minimal, but \((2,2)\) minimizes no positive weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive cost scalarization selects frontier points, but some discrete Pareto points may be unsupported by every positive weighting.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\subseteq\mathbb N^2\) is nonempty.
The scalarized minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{(u,v)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon}(\alpha u+\beta v)\subseteq\mathcal F_\varepsilon,\quad\text{while the reverse coverage need not hold.}
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Scalarization and Unsupported Frontier Points

assumptions_latex: All compared schedules address the same problem data and error tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
Both oracle counts are nonnegative integers.
Admissibility uses the declared deterministic oracle model and stopping guarantee.

children.title: Stochastic Sliding Interface
children.top_down_role: Navigation boundary to stochastic conditional-gradient sliding.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic Sample Accounting for Sliding Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level accounting for stochastic gradients used by outer sliding iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If outer iteration \(k\) uses a batch of \(b_k\) stochastic gradients, then through iteration \(K\) the stochastic first-order oracle count is \[N_{\mathrm{SFO}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^K b_k.\] Thus the number of batched outer updates equals the sample count only when every \(b_k=1\); inner LMO calls are counted separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Batched sliding costs the sum of all batch sizes in stochastic-gradient calls, not merely the number of outer iterations.
assumptions_latex: Each sampled gradient is charged as one stochastic first-order oracle call.
Inner LMO calls are a separate resource.

notation.meaning: Stochastic first-order oracle calls through iteration K.
Batch size at outer iteration k.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Sample Accounting for Sliding Batches

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for the inverse-batch variance guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conditionally centered errors \(Z_j\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\left\|b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^b Z_j\right\|_2^2\middle|y\right]=b^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^b\mathbb E[\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle\mid y].\] Conditional independence may be weakened to zero conditional cross-covariances. Marginal unbiasedness and variance bounds alone do not yield a \(1/b\) reduction: when \(Z_1=\cdots=Z_b=Z\), averaging leaves the conditional variance unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-batch variance reduction requires conditional decorrelation; perfectly correlated unbiased samples provide no reduction.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Z_j\) is square-integrable and conditionally centered.
For the inverse-batch guarantee, conditional cross-covariances vanish and \(\mathbb E[\|Z_j\|_2^2\mid y]\le\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[\|b^{-1}\sum_jZ_j\|_2^2\mid y]\le\sigma^2/b\text{ under conditional decorrelation, but not from marginal conditions alone.}

notation.meaning: Centered stochastic-gradient error in batch position j.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch Variance Reduction Requires Decorrelation
Stochastic Sliding Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean stochastic-oracle conditions permitting batch gradients to replace deterministic outer gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) lie in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\). A stochastic sliding interface supplies \(G(x,\xi)\) such that, for every \(x\in X\), \[\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla f(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert G(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\mid x]\le\sigma^2.\] At outer iteration \(k\), choose an integer \(b_k\ge1\), draw conditionally independent samples \(\xi_{k,1},\ldots,\xi_{k,b_k}\) at \(y_k\), and set \(\bar G_k=b_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(y_k,\xi_{k,j})\). The inner subproblem continues to access \(X\) only through a linear minimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Euclidean geometry, the stochastic interface supplies unbiased, bounded-variance batch gradients to outer sliding steps while the inner solves remain projection-free.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is contained in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\) is differentiable on \(X\).
Samples in each batch are conditionally independent given the query point, and \(b_k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\bar G_k\mid y_k]=\nabla f(y_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert\bar G_k-\nabla f(y_k)\rVert_2^2\mid y_k]\le\sigma^2/b_k\).

notation.meaning: Positive integer batch size at outer iteration k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Euclidean unbiased bounded-variance batch-gradient interface

children.title: Conditional-Gradient Sparsity Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Support growth, compression, and approximation families for atomic iterates.

children.title: Iteration-Wise Support Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation-size behavior under successive atom discovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-Wise Support Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-new-atom representation bound for standard conditional-gradient iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\), suppose \(x_0\) admits an atomic convex representation using at most \(s_0\) atoms, and generate \(x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_k+\gamma_k a_k\) with \(a_k\in\mathcal A\) and \(\gamma_k\in[0,1]\). Then, without compression, \(x_k\) admits a convex representation using at most \(s_0+k\) atoms. If \(\gamma_k=1\), the coefficients inherited from the preceding representation vanish; otherwise the update introduces at most the one atom \(a_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard conditional-gradient update adds at most one atom to a maintained representation, so an iterate after k updates has a representation using at most s0 plus k atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the convex hull of an atomic set \(\mathcal A\).
\(x_0\) admits a convex representation using at most \(s_0\) atoms.
Each update is a convex combination with one atom \(a_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every integer \(k\ge0\), \(x_k\) admits an atomic convex representation of cardinality at most \(s_0+k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct representation accounting for convex-combination updates

children.title: Carathéodory Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional support reduction and bounded atomic representations.

children.title: Exact Convex-Hull Compression
children.top_down_role: Support reduction preserving the represented feasible point.

assumptions_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^s\lambda_i a_i\) with every \(\lambda_i>0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\).
The atoms lie in an affine space of dimension \(r\), and \(s>r+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) has an exact convex representation with at most \(s-1\) positive coefficients, and repetition yields at most \(r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive support elimination from a finite convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x=\sum_{i=1}^s\lambda_i a_i\), \(\lambda_i>0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and \(s>r+1\) for atoms in an affine space of dimension \(r\), choose a nonzero affine dependence \(c\) satisfying \(\sum_i c_i a_i=0\) and \(\sum_i c_i=0\). After replacing \(c\) by \(-c\) if needed, set \(\theta=\min_{c_i>0}\lambda_i/c_i\) and \(\lambda_i'=\lambda_i-\theta c_i\). Then \(\lambda_i'\ge0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i'=1\), \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i'a_i\), and at least one coefficient vanishes. Repetition produces a representation with at most \(r+1\) atoms after at most \(s-r-1\) eliminations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine dependence among too many active atoms gives a coefficient direction along which one weight can be driven to zero without changing the represented point.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dependence Elimination

assumptions_latex: \(a_0,\ldots,a_r\) are affinely independent.
\(x\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}\{a_0,\ldots,a_r\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every convex representation of \(x\) using these vertices has support \(r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of the affine-dimension support bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_0,\ldots,a_r\) be affinely independent and let \(x\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}\{a_0,\ldots,a_r\}\). The barycentric coordinates of \(x\) are unique and all strictly positive. Consequently, \(x\) does not belong to the convex hull of any \(r\) of these vertices, so the universal \(r+1\) support bound in exact Carathéodory compression is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior point of an r-dimensional simplex requires all r+1 vertices, so the exact Carathéodory support bound cannot generally be lowered.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness on a Simplex
Exact Convex-Hull Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Carathéodory compression preserving the represented point exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\), and let \(r=\dim\operatorname{aff}(\mathcal A)\). Then there exist atoms \(a_0,\ldots,a_r\in\mathcal A\) and coefficients \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_r\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=0}^r\lambda_i=1\) and \[x=\sum_{i=0}^r\lambda_i a_i.\] Consequently, any finite convex representation of \(x\) with more than \(r+1\) positive coefficients can be replaced by one with at most \(r+1\) positive coefficients without changing \(x\); in particular, at most \(d+1\) atoms suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in an affine-dimension r convex hull has an exact convex representation using at most r plus one atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a subset of \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(x\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).
\(r=\dim\operatorname{aff}(\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an exact representation of \(x\) supported on at most \(r+1\le d+1\) atoms.

notation.meaning: Affine hull of the atomic set.
Affine dimension of the atomic set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is a correct finite-dimensional Carathéodory compression statement and fits the exact-compression leaf, but no authoritative theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Approximate Carathéodory Compression
children.top_down_role: Controlled approximation by reduced atomic support.

assumptions_latex: \(x=\sum_{j=1}^N p_j a_j\) is a finite convex representation in a real Hilbert space.
\(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) are independent with \(\mathbb P(A_i=a_j)=p_j\).

notation.meaning: diameter of the atoms in the supplied representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive randomized compression when a finite convex representation is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x=\sum_{j=1}^N p_j a_j\) in a real Hilbert space, draw \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) independently with \(\mathbb P(A_i=a_j)=p_j\) and return \(\widehat x_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m A_i\). Then \(\mathbb E\widehat x_m=x\) and \[\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|^2=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^Np_j\|a_j-x\|^2\le\frac{D^2}{m},\] where \(D=\max_{i,j}\|a_i-a_j\|\). Consequently, at least one realization uses at most \(m\) atoms and has error at most \(D/\sqrt m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling atoms independently from an existing convex representation and averaging them gives an unbiased m-atom compression with mean-square error at most D squared over m.
knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Atom-Sampling Compression

assumptions_latex: The ambient norm is \(\ell_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dimension-free Hilbert-rate compression for arbitrary Banach norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{2m}\}\subset\ell_1^{2m}\) and \(x=(2m)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{2m}e_i\). The atomic diameter is \(D=2\), and \[\inf\{\|x-y\|_1:y\in\operatorname{conv}(A),\ |\operatorname{supp}(y)|\le m\}=1.\] Thus no bound \(CD/\sqrt m\) with a universal constant \(C\) can hold in every normed space; the Hilbert-space assumption in the inverse-square-root compression theorem is substantive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an l1 simplex, the uniform point on 2m vertices stays distance one from every convex combination of at most m vertices, so Hilbert-rate compression does not extend to arbitrary norms.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Hilbert Compression Failure

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is bounded in a real Hilbert space.
\(x\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\).
\(m\ge 1\) is an integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_m\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\) supported on at most \(m\) atoms with \(\lVert x-x_m\rVert\le D/\sqrt m\).

notation.meaning: Diameter of the atomic set in the Hilbert norm.
Compressed convex combination using at most m atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-free compression in a Hilbert norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a bounded subset of a real Hilbert space, let \(D=\sup_{a,b\in A}\lVert a-b\rVert\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\). For every integer \(m\ge 1\), there exist atoms \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in A\) and coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) such that, for \(x_m=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i\), \[\lVert x-x_m\rVert\le \frac{D}{\sqrt m}.\] Thus, for \(\varepsilon>0\), an approximation of norm error at most \(\varepsilon\) uses at most \(\max\{1,\lceil D^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\}\) atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in a bounded convex hull has an m-atom approximation with Hilbert-norm error at most the atomic diameter divided by the square root of m.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Carathéodory Compression

children.title: Active-Set Support Control
children.top_down_role: Support behavior under away, pairwise, corrective, and pruning mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: The update is permitted to use atoms outside \(S_t\cup\{s_t\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of restricting correction to a one-atom enlargement of the current active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bound \(|S_{t+1}|\le |S_t|+1\) for a corrective step requires the correction to use no atoms outside \(S_t\cup\{s_t\}\). Without this restriction there is no one-step cardinality bound in terms of \(|S_t|\): for any \(q\ge1\), take the simplex atoms \(A=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{q+1}\}\), start from \(x_t=e_1\) with \(S_t=\{e_1\}\), and let an unrestricted correction return \(x_{t+1}=(q+1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{q+1}e_i\). Its unique simplex representation has \(|S_{t+1}|=q+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corrective step can add arbitrarily many atoms in one iteration unless its working set is restricted to the current active set plus the newly selected atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Unrestricted Correction Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) has a finite convex atomic representation over its positive-weight active set \(S_t\).
Forward, away, and pairwise step sizes preserve nonnegative coefficients summing to one.
Each corrective or pruning operation uses only atoms in \(S_t\cup\{s_t\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_{t+1}|\le |S_t|+1\), with support reductions possible when updated coefficients become zero.

notation.meaning: Positive-weight active set at iteration t.
Forward atom selected at iteration t.
Away atom selected from the active set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support changes induced by standard active-set conditional-gradient updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_t=\sum_{a\in S_t}\alpha_a^t a\), where \(S_t\subset A\) is finite, \(\alpha_a^t>0\), and \(\sum_{a\in S_t}\alpha_a^t=1\). A feasible Frank--Wolfe step toward \(s_t\in A\) satisfies \(S_{t+1}\subseteq S_t\cup\{s_t\}\). A feasible away step using \(v_t\in S_t\) introduces no atom outside \(S_t\) and may delete \(v_t\) when its updated coefficient becomes zero. A feasible pairwise step from \(v_t\in S_t\) toward \(s_t\in A\) introduces at most \(s_t\) and may delete \(v_t\). A corrective or pruning operation restricted to atoms in \(S_t\cup\{s_t\}\) also satisfies \(S_{t+1}\subseteq S_t\cup\{s_t\}\) after zero-weight atoms are removed. Hence \[|S_{t+1}|\le |S_t|+1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and pairwise steps add at most one atom, away steps add none, and corrective or pruning steps restricted to the current active set and selected forward atom preserve the same support-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Support Control

children.title: Sparsity–Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality associated with restricted atomic support.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is bounded in a real Hilbert space with diameter \(D\).
\(f\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\).
A minimizer \(x^*\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\) exists.

notation.meaning: best objective value among convex combinations of at most m atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of normwise sparse approximation to objective-value accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) have Hilbert-norm diameter \(D\), let \(f\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\), and let \(x^*\) minimize \(f\) there. If \[f_m^*=\inf\{f(y):y\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\text{ has a representation using at most }m\text{ atoms}\},\] then \[0\le f_m^*-f(x^*)\le\frac{MD}{\sqrt m}.\] Therefore \(m\ge\max\{1,\lceil M^2D^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\}\) suffices for objective error at most \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an M-Lipschitz objective, the Hilbert norm compression law yields an m-atom objective gap at most MD divided by the square root of m.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Objective Tradeoff

assumptions_latex: The atoms are the standard orthonormal basis vectors of \(\ell_2^N\).

notation.meaning: uniform point in the convex hull of the orthogonal atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order sharpness of the universal inverse-square-root norm tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{e_1,\ldots,e_N\}\subset\ell_2^N\), let \(x=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Ne_i\), and let \(1\le m<N\). Then the best convex combination supported on at most \(m\) atoms has equal weights on some \(m\) coordinates and satisfies \[e_m(x)=\sqrt{\frac1m-\frac1N}.\] Taking \(N\ge2m\) gives \(e_m(x)\ge1/\sqrt{2m}\), so the universal \(m^{-1/2}\) Hilbert-norm rate cannot be improved in order without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform point on many orthogonal atoms has best m-atom error of order one over the square root of m, matching the universal upper rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal-Atom Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is bounded in a real Hilbert space.
\(x\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\).
\(m\ge 1\) is an integer.
Accuracy is measured in the Hilbert norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_m(x)\le D/\sqrt m\), hence \(m\ge\max\{1,\lceil D^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\}\) suffices for \(e_m(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Best error among convex combinations of at most m atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic support required for Hilbert-norm approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a bounded subset of a real Hilbert space with diameter \(D\), and, for every integer \(m\ge 1\), define the best \(m\)-atom error of \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(A)\) by \[e_m(x)=\inf\left\{\left\lVert x-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i a_i\right\rVert:a_i\in A,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Then \(e_m(x)\le D/\sqrt m\). Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the support budget \(m\ge\max\{1,\lceil D^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\}\) suffices for error at most \(\varepsilon\). For positive \(D\), the resulting universal support upper bound scales as \(O(D^2/\varepsilon^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded Hilbert-space atoms, m-term convex approximation has error at most D divided by the square root of m, so positive accuracy ε is achieved with at most the larger of one and the ceiling of D²/ε² atoms.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity–Accuracy Tradeoffs

children.title: Structured Atomic Representations
children.top_down_role: Interpretations of atomic support as coordinate sparsity, matrix rank, or mixture complexity.

children.title: Coordinate-Group Support Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Atomic models encoding coordinate and grouped supports.

children.title: Coordinate-Sparse Representations
children.top_down_role: Atomic representations built from individual coordinate supports.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^d\)
\(0\le k\le d\)
Approximation error is measured in \(\ell_2\).

notation.meaning: an index set of k largest-magnitude coordinates
hard-thresholded vector retaining coordinates in the selected set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best Euclidean approximation under a prescribed coordinate-support budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(0\le k\le d\), let \(I_k\) contain indices of \(k\) largest values of \(|x_i|\), with arbitrary tie breaking, and define \((H_k(x))_i=x_i\) for \(i\in I_k\) and zero otherwise. Then \[H_k(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z:\|z\|_0\le k}\|x-z\|_2,\qquad \|x-H_k(x)\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin I_k}|x_i|^2.\] A top-k set can be found in \(O(d)\) comparison time by deterministic selection, or in \(O(d\log d)\) time by sorting. Ties may make the minimizing support nonunique without changing the optimal error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping the k largest-magnitude coordinates gives a best k-coordinate-sparse Euclidean approximation, whose squared error is exactly the discarded coordinate tail.
knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Thresholding Representation
Coordinate-Sparse Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic representation using signed coordinate directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), its coordinate support is \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{i:x_i\ne0\}\), and \(x\) is \(k\)-coordinate-sparse when \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le k\). With signed coordinate atoms \(A=\{\pm e_i:1\le i\le d\}\), every nonzero \(x\) admits the conic representation \[x=\sum_{i\in\operatorname{supp}(x)}|x_i|\,\operatorname{sgn}(x_i)e_i.\] Moreover, if \(\lVert x\rVert_1\le\tau\), then \(x\in\tau\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})\), and the number of nonzero coordinate atoms equals \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is k-coordinate-sparse when at most k coordinates are nonzero; signed coordinate atoms give one active atom for each nonzero coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
\(e_i\) denotes the ith standard basis vector.

notation.meaning: Indices of the nonzero coordinates of x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and signed-coordinate representation fit the leaf and are mathematically standard, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the atomic representation claim.

children.title: Group-Sparse Representations
children.top_down_role: Atomic representations built from predefined or structured support groups.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latent Group Atomic Gauge and Polar
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex atomic representation induced by group-supported Euclidean atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal G}\{a\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{supp}(a)\subseteq G,\ \|a\|_2\le1\}\). Then
\[\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf_{\substack{x=\sum_{G\in\mathcal G}z_G\\\operatorname{supp}(z_G)\subseteq G}}\sum_{G\in\mathcal G}\|z_G\|_2,\qquad \gamma_{\mathcal A}^{\circ}(y)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G}\|y_G\|_2.\]
If the groups cover every coordinate, \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is finite everywhere. Overlapping groups may yield nonunique minimizing decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The group-atomic gauge is the minimum sum of group-component norms, and its polar is the largest Euclidean norm of a group restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a finite family of nonempty coordinate subsets.
The atoms are Euclidean-unit vectors supported within individual groups.

notation.meaning: Union of group-supported Euclidean unit balls.
Gauge generated by the group atoms.
Latent component supported in group G.

knowledge_statements.title: Latent Group Atomic Gauge and Polar
Group-Sparse Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representations supported on a small number of coordinate groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) be a finite family of subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A vector \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) has a \(k\)-group-sparse representation relative to \(\mathcal G\) if there exist groups \(G_1,\ldots,G_r\in\mathcal G\) and vectors \(z_j\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \(r\le k\), \(\operatorname{supp}(z_j)\subseteq G_j\), and \[x=\sum_{j=1}^{r}z_j.\] The group support complexity is the minimum such \(r\). This definition permits overlapping groups; consequently, the minimizing decomposition need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is k-group-sparse if it decomposes into at most k vectors, each supported inside one prescribed coordinate group.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a finite family of coordinate subsets.
\(x\in\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is \(k\)-group-sparse iff it has a group-supported decomposition with at most \(k\) nonzero terms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the group-sparse representation leaf and explicitly permits overlaps, but it has no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Support-Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representational consequences of coordinate-level versus group-level atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of incidence-based group counts to equal latent group complexity under overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}\) and \(x=e_2\in\mathbb R^3\). Both restrictions \(x_{\{1,2\}}\) and \(x_{\{2,3\}}\) are nonzero, so the active-group incidence count is two. Nevertheless, \(x\) is supported in either single group and has minimum group-decomposition complexity one. Thus the partition inequalities cannot be extended to overlapping groups by counting all nonzero group restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With overlapping groups, counting nonzero group restrictions can exceed the minimum number of group-supported components.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed group family may overlap.
Incidence count includes every group whose restriction of x is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlap Invalidates Incidence Counting
Support-Granularity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of coordinate and group support counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) be a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) into groups of size at most \(q\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), define \(s_c(x)=|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\) and \(s_g(x)=|\{G\in\mathcal G:x_G\ne0\}|\). Then \[s_g(x)\le s_c(x)\le q\,s_g(x).\] Thus a group atom may activate as many as \(q\) coordinates while counting as one support unit. Bounds expressed in group support can therefore be smaller by a factor up to \(q\), at the cost of coarser localization within active groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For groups of size at most q, active-group count is no larger than coordinate support, which is at most q times the active-group count.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) partitions the coordinates.
Every group has cardinality at most \(q\).
\(x\in\mathbb R^d\).

notation.meaning: Number of groups containing a nonzero coordinate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-count inequalities are correct for a partition into nonempty groups of size at most q and the property kind fits the tradeoff leaf, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Low-Rank Matrix Representations
children.top_down_role: Matrix iterates generated from rank-structured atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite specialization of low-rank atomic representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\succeq0\) with spectral decomposition \(X=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i u_i u_i^{\mathsf T}\), \(\lambda_i>0\),
\[\operatorname{tr}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i,\qquad \{X\succeq0:\operatorname{tr}(X)\le\tau\}=\tau\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{uu^{\mathsf T}:\|u\|_2=1\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).\]
The decomposition uses \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\) rank-one PSD atoms, and any sum of \(k\) such atoms has rank at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD trace ball is the convex hull of scaled rank-one projectors, and atomic support bounds rank.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: PSD Trace-Ball Atomic Representation
Low-Rank Matrix Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nuclear-norm domains represented by rank-one atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{uv^{\mathsf T}:\lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert v\rVert_2=1\}\) in \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). If \(X\) has compact singular-value decomposition \(X=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\), then \[\lVert X\rVert_*=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i,\qquad X\in\tau\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \lVert X\rVert_*\le\tau.\] The displayed decomposition uses \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\) rank-one atoms. Hence a conditional-gradient iterate formed from at most \(k\) such atoms has rank at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nuclear-norm ball is the convex hull of scaled rank-one unit atoms, and a combination of k such atoms has rank at most k.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{X:\lVert X\rVert_*\le\tau\}=\tau\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})\), and atomic support \(k\) implies rank at most \(k\).

notation.meaning: Nuclear norm, the sum of singular values.
Set of unit rank-one matrix atoms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nuclear-norm convex-hull representation and rank bound fit the representation leaf, but the record provides no authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Finite-Support Measure Representations
children.top_down_role: Finite atomic approximations within measure and continuous-dictionary domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological boundary for finite support on a merely measurable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a measurable space without a topology, define the atomic support cardinality of \(\mu\) as the least \(r\) for which \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^r w_i\delta_{\theta_i}\) with distinct \(\theta_i\) and positive weights. This is an algebraic atomic representation and must not be identified with topological support unless a topology and its associated measurable structure have been specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite Dirac-mixture cardinality is well defined on a measurable space, whereas topological support requires additional topology.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is a measurable space and all Dirac measures used are defined on its sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite atomic cardinality is meaningful without topology; topological support is not.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Versus Topological Support

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dirac Measures as Extreme Points on Standard Borel Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point interpretation of measure atoms under a sufficient measurable-space assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\Theta\) is a standard Borel space, then
\[\operatorname{ext}(\mathcal P(\Theta))=\{\delta_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}.\]
Consequently, finite convex combinations of extreme points are exactly finite Dirac mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a standard Borel space, the extreme probability measures are precisely the Dirac measures.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is a standard Borel space.
\(\mathcal P(\Theta)\) is the convex set of probability measures on its Borel sigma-algebra.

notation.meaning: Convex set of probability measures on Theta.

knowledge_statements.title: Dirac Measures as Extreme Points on Standard Borel Spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support reduction preserving an attained finite-dimensional feature barycenter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y=\int_\Theta\phi(\theta)\,d\mu(\theta)\in\mathbb R^p\). If \(y\in\operatorname{conv}(\phi(\Theta))\), then there exist \(r\le p+1\), points \(\theta_i\in\Theta\), and weights \(w_i\ge0\) summing to one such that
\[y=\sum_{i=1}^r w_i\phi(\theta_i)=\int_\Theta\phi\,d\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^r w_i\delta_{\theta_i}\Bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any attained p-dimensional feature barycenter has a moment-equivalent probability measure with at most p+1 atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^p\) is measurable and integrable under \(\mu\).
\(y=\int\phi\,d\mu\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\phi(\Theta))\), not merely its closure.

notation.meaning: Weights of the reduced atomic measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Moment Support Reduction
Finite-Support Measure Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic representation of probability measures by Dirac masses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a measurable space. A probability measure \(\mu\) has finite support of size at most \(k\) precisely when there exist \(r\le k\), points \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\in\Theta\), and weights \(w_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_i=1\) such that \[\mu=\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_i\delta_{\theta_i}.\] For every measurable integrable test function \(\varphi\), this representation gives \(\int_\Theta\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_{i=1}^{r}w_i\varphi(\theta_i)\). Thus the Dirac measures are the atoms and \(r\) is the atomic support complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely supported probability measure is exactly a convex combination of finitely many Dirac masses, with integration reduced to a weighted finite sum.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is a measurable space.
\(\mu\) is a probability measure on \(\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{supp}(\mu)|\le k\) iff \(\mu\) is a convex combination of at most \(k\) Dirac measures.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure concentrated at θ.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite Dirac-mixture characterization fits the leaf, but no source is cited. A source should also establish the intended meaning of finite support on a merely measurable space, where topological support is unavailable.

children.title: Polyhedral Atomic Interfaces
