children.title: Stochastic-Gradient Regime
children.top_down_role: Interface to conditional-gradient settings using noisy or sampled gradient information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbiased Gradients Do Not Make Naive LMO Directions Unbiased
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a raw one-sample linear-oracle update under unbiased bounded-variance gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[-1,1]\) and \(F(x)=x\), whose unique minimizer is \(-1\). Let independent stochastic gradients satisfy \(G_t=-1\) with probability \(3/4\) and \(G_t=7\) with probability \(1/4\). Then \(\mathbb E[G_t]=1=F'(x)\) and \(G_t\) has finite variance, but the exact stochastic linear minimizer is \(s_t=-\operatorname{sign}(G_t)\), so \(\mathbb E[s_t]=1/2\). If \(\gamma_t\in(0,1]\), \(\sum_t\gamma_t=\infty\), and \(\sum_t\gamma_t^2<\infty\), then \(x_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)x_t+\gamma_t s_t\) converges almost surely to \(1/2\), not to \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased finite-variance gradient sample can induce systematically biased LMO atoms, causing a naive one-sample stochastic Frank-Wolfe recursion to converge to a nonoptimal point.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic gradients are independent across iterations.
\(\gamma_t\in(0,1]\), \(\sum_t\gamma_t=\infty\), and \(\sum_t\gamma_t^2<\infty\).
The linear minimization oracle is solved exactly for every sampled gradient.

notation.meaning: Exact LMO atom selected from the sampled gradient.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Gradients Do Not Make Naive LMO Directions Unbiased
Stochastic-Gradient Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-model boundary for conditional-gradient updates using sampled gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\phi(x;\xi)]\) on a compact convex set \(C\). A stochastic-gradient conditional-gradient regime supplies, at iteration \(t\), a random vector \(G_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|G_t-\nabla F(x_t)\|_*^2\mid x_t]\leq\sigma^2\). The method computes \(s_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle G_t,s\rangle\) and updates \(x_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)x_t+\gamma_t s_t\). Performance is measured in expectation or probability and counts both stochastic samples and linear-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stochastic-gradient regime uses an unbiased, bounded-variance gradient sample inside each linear oracle and evaluates convergence probabilistically while separately counting samples and oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(F\) is differentiable on \(C\).
\(0\leq\gamma_t\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed oracle and convex-combination update define the stochastic-gradient conditional-gradient regime.

children.title: Finite-Sum Regime
children.top_down_role: Interface to objectives structured as finite collections of component functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-gradient model with a fixed, reusable collection of component objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-sum conditional-gradient problem has the form \(\min_{x\in C}F(x)\), where \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is compact and convex, and component gradients \(\nabla f_i(x)\) are individually queryable. An iteration may form the full gradient at cost \(n\) component-gradient evaluations or a sampled estimator from selected indices, then call \(s_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle G_t,s\rangle\). Unlike a general expectation model, the fixed index set permits repeated access, stored reference gradients, and variance-reduced estimators; complexity therefore records component-gradient evaluations separately from linear-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-sum regime averages a fixed set of reusable component functions, enabling full gradients or repeated-index estimators while separately counting component and linear-oracle work.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each \(f_i\) is differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) with reusable component-gradient access defines the finite-sum regime.

notation.meaning: full or sampled gradient estimator used by the oracle

children.title: Variance-Reduced Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary with variance-reduction mechanisms used in conditional-gradient methods.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbiased Costs Do Not Commute with the LMO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinearity boundary for using an unbiased random gradient estimator inside a linear minimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every integrable random covector \(V\) and nonempty compact domain \(C\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{s\in C}\langle V,s\rangle\right]\leq \min_{s\in C}\langle\mathbb EV,s\rangle.
\]
The inequality can be strict: if \(C=[-1,1]\) and \(V\in\{-1,1\}\) with equal probabilities, then \(\mathbb EV=0\), while \(\mathbb E[\min_{s\in C}Vs]=-1<0\). Thus estimator unbiasedness does not imply unbiasedness of the selected LMO atom or attained LMO value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimization and expectation do not generally commute, so an unbiased gradient estimator can produce a biased LMO output and attained value.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and compact.
\(V\) is an integrable random covector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\min_{s\in C}\langle V,s\rangle]\leq\min_{s\in C}\langle\mathbb EV,s\rangle\), with possible strict inequality.

notation.meaning: random variance-reduced cost vector supplied to the LMO

children.title: Sampling-Oracle Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between sampling effort, gradient quality, and linear-oracle usage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population correction for the gradient-quality versus component-oracle tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq2\), fix vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) in a Euclidean space, set \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\), and sample a size-\(b\) subset \(B\) uniformly without replacement, where \(1\leq b\leq n\). For \(\widehat g_B=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}g_i\), \[\mathbb E[\widehat g_B]=\bar g,\qquad \mathbb E\|\widehat g_B-\bar g\|^2=\frac{n-b}{b(n-1)}\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|g_i-\bar g\|^2\right).\] The batch uses \(b\) component calls and one subsequent linear-oracle call, with zero sampling variance at \(b=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform sampling without replacement has finite-population variance factor (n-b)/(b(n-1)), costs b component calls, and becomes exact for a full batch.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\) and \(1\leq b\leq n\).
\(B\) is a uniformly random size-\(b\) subset.
The norm is induced by an inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Mini-Batch Variance
Sampling-Oracle Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batching exchanges stochastic-gradient precision for component-oracle work without reducing linear-oracle count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose independent stochastic gradients \(G(x;\xi_j)\) satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[G(x;\xi_j)]=
abla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}\|G(x;\xi_j)-
abla F(x)\|_*^2\leq\sigma^2\). For the batch estimator \( ar G_b=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^bG(x;\xi_j)\), independence gives \(\mathbb{E}\| ar G_b-
abla F(x)\|_*^2\leq\sigma^2/b\) in a Hilbert norm. A conditional-gradient iteration using \( ar G_b\) consumes \(b\) stochastic-gradient samples but still one linear minimization oracle call. Thus increasing \(b\) lowers variance by a factor \(b\) while increasing sampling work by the same factor, leaving the iteration's linear-oracle count unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch of size b divides gradient variance by b but multiplies sample cost by b, while each conditional-gradient iteration still makes one linear-oracle call.
assumptions_latex: The sampled gradient errors are independent and conditionally mean zero.
The norm is induced by an inner product.
Each sample has second moment at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Batch size \(b\) yields variance at most \(\sigma^2/b\), costs \(b\) samples, and requires one linear-oracle call per iteration.

children.title: Partial-Feedback Regime Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interface to regret and bandit-feedback analyses.

children.title: Online-Feedback Regime
children.top_down_role: Interface to sequential conditional-gradient settings with progressively revealed losses.

knowledge_statements.title: Online-Feedback Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential full-gradient feedback with regret, rather than offline suboptimality, as the performance criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and convex. At round \(t\), an online conditional-gradient learner chooses \(x_t\in C\) before observing a convex loss \(\ell_t:C\to\mathbb{R}\), incurs \(\ell_t(x_t)\), and then receives a subgradient \(g_t\in\partial\ell_t(x_t)\). Full first-order feedback permits a linear-oracle call such as \(s_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g_t,s\rangle\) followed by a feasible convex-combination update. Performance after \(T\) rounds is measured by static regret \(\operatorname{Reg}_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x_t)-\min_{x\in C}\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x)\), not by suboptimality for one fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the online-feedback regime, each decision precedes its convex loss, a subgradient arrives afterward, and performance is cumulative regret against the best fixed feasible decision.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Every \(\ell_t\) is convex on \(C\).
The full subgradient \(g_t\) is revealed after round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relevant criterion is \(\operatorname{Reg}_T\), with decisions made before observing the corresponding losses.

notation.meaning: loss revealed at online round t
revealed subgradient at the played decision

children.title: Bandit-Feedback Regime
children.top_down_role: Interface to settings where optimization proceeds from restricted function feedback.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Domain Shrinkage for Perturbed Queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric condition ensuring that spherical bandit perturbations remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is convex and \(r\mathbb B^d\subseteq C\) for some \(r>0\). For \(0\leq\delta\leq r\), define \(C_\delta=(1-\delta/r)C\). Then \(C_\delta+\delta\mathbb B^d\subseteq C\); in particular, \(x\pm\delta u\in C\) for every \(x\in C_\delta\) and \(u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a convex feasible set containing a centered radius-r ball ensures that every radius-delta perturbation remains feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex.
\(r\mathbb B^d\subseteq C\).
\(0\leq\delta\leq r\).
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Domain Shrinkage for Perturbed Queries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-value symmetric counterpart of the one-point smoothed-gradient interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb S^{d-1})\), let \(f\) be locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood containing \(x+\delta\mathbb B^d\), and define \(f_\delta(x)=\mathbb E_{v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb B^d)}[f(x+\delta v)]\). If both queries are admissible, then \[\widehat g^{(2)}(x,u)=\frac{d}{2\delta}\bigl(f(x+\delta u)-f(x-\delta u)\bigr)u\] satisfies \(\mathbb E_u[\widehat g^{(2)}(x,u)]=\nabla f_\delta(x)\). It costs two value queries and does not generally estimate \(\nabla f(x)\) without smoothing bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric two-point estimator uses two feasible value queries and is unbiased for the ball-smoothed gradient, not generally for the original gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta\mathbb B^d\).
\(x\pm\delta u\) are admissible almost surely.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Two-Point Bandit Estimator
Bandit-Feedback Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-point value feedback replaces the exact-gradient oracle used by standard conditional-gradient updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(u_t\) be uniform on the unit sphere, and suppose the learner observes only \(f_t(x_t+\delta u_t)\). The estimator \(\widehat g_t=(d/\delta)f_t(x_t+\delta u_t)u_t\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla f_{t,\delta}(x_t)\), where \(f_{t,\delta}\) is the ball-smoothed loss, rather than generally equaling \(\nabla f_t(x_t)\). Consequently, a linear minimization oracle called with \(\widehat g_t\) implements a noisy conditional-gradient step for a smoothed objective; its analysis requires smoothing bias, estimator variance, and feasibility of the perturbed query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-point bandit feedback yields a noisy gradient of a smoothed loss, so conditional-gradient guarantees require explicit control of smoothing, variance, and query feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f_t\) is integrable on a \(\delta\)-neighborhood of \(C\).
\(x_t+\delta u_t\) is an admissible query almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla f_{t,\delta}(x_t)\), not necessarily \(\nabla f_t(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: Ball-smoothed version of the round-t loss.
Random unit direction used for the bandit query.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the bandit-feedback leaf, and the one-point estimator claim is mathematically standard under an independent uniform sphere direction and an explicitly defined ball smoothing. However, no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the smoothing identity, bias/variance interface, or perturbed-query requirement. An authoritative bandit optimization source with a specific theorem, lemma, section, or page is required.

children.title: Regret-Analysis Interface
children.top_down_role: Chapter boundary connecting conditional-gradient behavior to regret-based performance criteria.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers expected online regret to offline stochastic objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_T\) be i.i.d. integrable convex random losses with \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f_t(x)]\), and let \(x_t\in C\) be measurable with respect to information available before \(f_t\) is observed. If \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\), then \[\mathbb E[F(\bar x_T)]-\min_{x\in C}F(x)\leq\frac1T\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{x\in C}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For i.i.d. convex losses, averaging adapted online decisions converts expected static regret divided by the horizon into expected offline suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex.
The losses are i.i.d., integrable, and convex.
\(x_t\) is selected before observing \(f_t\).
A minimizer of \(F\) over \(C\) exists.

notation.meaning: Arithmetic mean of the online decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Online-to-Batch Conversion
Regret-Analysis Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex online losses reduce regret control to linearized losses consumed by a conditional-gradient subroutine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decisions \(x_t\in C\), differentiable convex losses \(f_t:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and every comparator \(x\in C\), convexity gives \(f_t(x_t)-f_t(x)\leq\langle\nabla f_t(x_t),x_t-x\rangle\). Hence the static regret satisfies \[\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{x\in C}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x)\leq\max_{x\in C}\sum_{t=1}^T\langle\nabla f_t(x_t),x_t-x\rangle.\] Thus a regret guarantee for the online linearized problems transfers directly to the original convex losses; without convexity, this reduction need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex losses, actual static regret is bounded by linearized regret, providing the formal interface between online analysis and conditional-gradient updates.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and convex.
Each \(f_t:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and convex.
\(x_t\in C\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\).

notation.meaning: Convex loss revealed on round t.
Static regret against the best fixed comparator in C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits this interface leaf, and the convexity inequality correctly transfers a bound on linearized regret to static regret for differentiable convex losses. No source or inspectable locator supports the stated reduction, so an authoritative online convex optimization reference with a specific section, theorem, or page is required.

children.title: Feedback-Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by the amount and quality of information available per decision round.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Error Propagates Through the Linear Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative conversion from restricted-feedback gradient error to approximate linear-oracle error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) have diameter \(D\) in \(\|\cdot\|\), let \(\widehat g=g+e\), and choose \(\widehat s\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle\widehat g,s\rangle\) and \(s^\star\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\). Then \[\langle g,\widehat s\rangle-\langle g,s^\star\rangle\leq D\|e\|_*.\] Thus an exact oracle call for the estimated gradient is only an additive-\(D\|e\|_*\) approximate call for the desired gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient error of dual norm eta can make the selected atom at most diameter times eta suboptimal for the true linear model.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and compact.
\(D=\sup_{x,y\in C}\|x-y\|<\infty\).
The displayed linear minimizers exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Error Propagates Through the Linear Oracle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Value Feedback Does Not Identify an Unrestricted Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens the nonspanning-query seed: even spanning finitely many value-query displacements is insufficient without function-class structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) and finitely many value-query points \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\). For every differentiable \(f\), there exists a polynomial \(h\) satisfying \(h(y_i)=0\) for every \(i\) and \(\nabla h(x)\neq0\). Hence \(f\) and \(f+h\) give identical answers at all queried points but have different gradients at \(x\). Therefore no finite collection of exact function values determines the gradient of an unrestricted differentiable function, even when the query displacements span \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many exact function values cannot identify the gradient of an unrestricted differentiable function, even when the query directions span the ambient space.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many function values are observed.
The admissible function class contains differentiable polynomial perturbations.
No structural restriction such as affinity or a known finite-dimensional model is imposed.

notation.meaning: Smooth perturbation vanishing at every queried point but having nonzero gradient at the target point.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Value Feedback Does Not Identify an Unrestricted Gradient
Feedback-Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fewer than full-dimensional value probes cannot identify an unrestricted local gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and value-query points \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\). If \(V=\operatorname{span}\{y_i-x:1\leq i\leq m\}
eq\mathbb{R}^d\), choose nonzero \(a\in V^\perp\). For any differentiable function \(f\), define \(\widetilde f(z)=f(z)+\langle a,z-xangle\). Then \(\widetilde f(y_i)=f(y_i)\) for every query, while \(
abla\widetilde f(x)=
abla f(x)+a\). Therefore these value observations cannot determine the exact gradient, and an exact gradient-based linear-minimization direction requires additional structure, random estimation, or sufficiently rich feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value queries whose displacement directions do not span the ambient space cannot identify the exact gradient needed by a standard conditional-gradient oracle call.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(x\).
\(V=\operatorname{span}\{y_i-x\}_{i=1}^m\) is a proper subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).

Orthogonal complement of the query-displacement span.

children.title: Distributed Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interface to network, consensus, and communication analyses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between separable local linear minimization and a coupled consensus oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C_{\mathrm{prod}}=\prod_{i=1}^n C_i\), \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C_{\mathrm{prod}}}\sum_{i=1}^n\langle g_i,s_i\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^n\operatorname*{argmin}_{u_i\in C_i}\langle g_i,u_i\rangle.\] For the consensus set \(C_{\mathrm{con}}=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n):s_1=\cdots=s_n=u,\ u\in C_0\}\), however, the global oracle is \[u^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C_0}\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^n g_i,u\right\rangle.\] For \(C_0=[-1,1]\), \(g_1=1\), and \(g_2=-1\), the independent outputs \((-1,1)\) violate consensus, while every common \(u\in[-1,1]\) minimizes the coupled objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LMOs decompose over Cartesian products, but consensus constraints require aggregating local costs; independent local minimizers can be globally infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is nonempty and compact.
All displayed linear minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LMO over \(\prod_iC_i\) decomposes blockwise, whereas the LMO over \(C_{\mathrm{con}}\) depends on \(\sum_i g_i\).

notation.meaning: local linear cost at agent i

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Oracle Decomposition Boundary
Distributed Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local conditional-gradient steps require a separate communication mechanism to enforce network agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) stack agent iterates and let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be doubly stochastic. Writing \(J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}/n\), one consensus round gives \(X^+=WX\) and \[\|(I-J)X^+\|_F\leq\|W-J\|_2\,\|(I-J)X\|_F.\] Thus geometric disagreement contraction requires \(\|W-J\|_2<1\). In particular, with \(W=I\), independently executed local linear-minimization and conditional-gradient steps need not approach consensus, so centralized convergence guarantees do not transfer without connectivity, mixing, and communication-complexity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed conditional-gradient analysis needs a contracting consensus operator; independent local oracle steps alone do not ensure agreement or centralized convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is doubly stochastic.
\(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) contains one row per agent.
The communication step is \(X^+=WX\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate for the distributed interface. The displayed contraction follows for a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, and the identity-matrix case correctly illustrates the absence of guaranteed disagreement contraction. The inventory locator does not support this consensus claim, and no relevant source is attached; a distributed optimization or consensus reference with a specific theorem, section, or page is required.

children.title: Nonconvex Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interface to nonconvex stationarity and stochastic nonconvex variants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth nonconvex conditional-gradient descent measured by the minimum Frank–Wolfe stationarity gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every iteration, smoothness and exact linear minimization give \[f(x_{t+1})\leq f(x_t)-\gamma g_{\mathrm{FW}}(x_t)+\frac{LD^2}{2}\gamma^2.\] Consequently, for any lower bound \(f_{\inf}\leq\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\), \[\min_{0\leq t<T}g_{\mathrm{FW}}(x_t)\leq\frac{f(x_0)-f_{\inf}}{T\gamma}+\frac{LD^2}{2}\gamma.\] Optimizing a constant \(\gamma\in(0,1]\) gives an \(O(T^{-1/2})\) minimum-gap bound and hence \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iterations for \(g_{\mathrm{FW}}\leq\varepsilon\), outside the initial capped-stepsize regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth nonconvex Frank–Wolfe descent attains a best-iterate stationarity gap of order one over the square root of the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex with Euclidean diameter \(D\).
\(f\) is differentiable, bounded below on \(C\), and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\).
\(s_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x_t),s\rangle\).
\(x_{t+1}=x_t+\gamma(s_t-x_t)\), where \(0<\gamma\leq1\).

notation.meaning: lower bound for f on C

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Frank–Wolfe Gap Complexity
Nonconvex Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Frank–Wolfe gap remains stationary but ceases to certify global suboptimality without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) on a nonempty compact convex set \(C\), define \(g_{\mathrm{FW}}(x)=\max_{v\in C}\langle\nabla f(x),x-v\rangle\). Then \(g_{\mathrm{FW}}(x)=0\) is equivalent to the first-order stationarity condition \(\langle\nabla f(x),v-x\rangle\geq0\) for all \(v\in C\). Global optimality does not follow when \(f\) is nonconvex: for \(C=[-2,2]\) and \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\), one has \(g_{\mathrm{FW}}(0)=0\), but \(f(0)=1>0=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In nonconvex problems, a zero Frank–Wolfe gap certifies first-order stationarity but not global optimality, as a concrete quartic example demonstrates.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\mathrm{FW}}(x)=0\) certifies stationarity, but without convexity it does not imply \(f(x)=\min_{v\in C}f(v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the nonconvex leaf. The Frank-Wolfe gap equivalence with constrained first-order stationarity is correct, and the quartic example correctly disproves global optimality. The supplied inventory concerns proximal-gradient analysis rather than nonconvex conditional gradients, so a relevant source with a specific theorem, definition, section, or page is required.

children.title: Related Greedy-Method Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interface to matching pursuit, continuous greedy, and substantially modified conditional-gradient constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes continuous greedy from conditional-gradient minimization despite their shared linear-optimization primitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A standard conditional-gradient minimization step selects \(s_t\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x_t),s\rangle\) and forms \(x_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)x_t+\gamma_t s_t\). Continuous greedy for monotone diminishing-returns maximization over a down-closed relaxation \(P\) instead selects \(v(t)\in\arg\max_{v\in P}\langle\nabla F(x(t)),v\rangle\) and follows \(\dot x(t)=v(t)\). Sharing a linear-optimization oracle does not identify the methods because their objective classes, oracle signs, trajectories, and performance criteria differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous greedy shares linear optimization with conditional gradient but belongs to monotone diminishing-returns maximization and follows an additive trajectory.
assumptions_latex: The conditional-gradient side is the standard convex-minimization update.
The continuous-greedy side is monotone diminishing-returns maximization over a down-closed convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shared linear-optimization access alone does not identify continuous greedy with conditional-gradient minimization.

notation.meaning: Down-closed relaxation used by continuous greedy.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Greedy Ownership Boundary
Related Greedy-Method Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive atom selection is not generally a feasibility-preserving conditional-gradient update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conditional-gradient step on a convex set \(C\) has the form \(x^+=(1-\gamma)x+\gamma s\), where \(x,s\in C\) and \(\gamma\in[0,1]\); convexity guarantees \(x^+\in C\). A matching-pursuit-style additive step \(x^+=x+\gamma s\) has no such guarantee. For the simplex \(C=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^2_+:z_1+z_2=1\}\), taking \(x=(1,0)\), \(s=(0,1)\), and \(\gamma>0\) gives \(x+\gamma s=(1,\gamma)\notin C\), whereas \((1-\gamma)x+\gamma s\in C\) for \(\gamma\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional-gradient convex combinations preserve feasibility, whereas additive greedy or matching-pursuit updates can leave the feasible set even when the selected atom is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex.
\(x,s\in C\).
\(\gamma\in[0,1]\) for the conditional-gradient update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-\gamma)x+\gamma s\in C\), but \(x+\gamma s\in C\) is not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the interface to related greedy methods. The convex-combination feasibility statement and simplex counterexample are correct, but no source or inspectable locator supports the characterization of the additive update as a matching-pursuit-style boundary. A relevant conditional-gradient or matching-pursuit reference with a specific section, theorem, or page is required.
